mfg1-mechanical-lesson-001.title: Stop and report when you notice an abnormal condition
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-001.objective:
Distinguish normal and abnormal conditions.
Briefly report the facts you observed.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
Familiarity alone cannot determine whether a machine is safe. Before work, confirm the equipment you are responsible for, the procedure, how to stop it, and whom to contact. Do not operate an unfamiliar machine or one whose controls you do not understand on your own initiative.
If you notice an unusual sound, smell, or vibration during work, give priority to preventing danger from spreading rather than finding a reason to continue. Stop the machine using the prescribed procedure and notify the person responsible from a safe position. Never put your hand into a running machine to remove chips or parts.
When reporting, state the equipment name, when you noticed the condition, the facts observed, and the action already taken. Saying only “I think it is broken” makes it difficult for the listener to assess the situation. Separate assumptions from facts if the cause is not yet confirmed. Even after stopping, do not restart the machine or open a cover to investigate without permission.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
During a cutting operation, vibration becomes stronger than usual. No obvious scratch is yet visible on the product.
1. Stop the work safely and move away from rotating parts.
2. Report: “Machine 2 has been vibrating strongly since about 10:15. It has been stopped. The cause has not yet been confirmed.”
3. Wait for the responsible person’s instructions and explain which products may have been affected.
The absence of a visible scratch does not establish that the equipment’s abnormal condition has disappeared. Checking the product and deciding whether to restart the equipment are separate decisions.

terms.meaning: A condition that differs from normal and needs checking.
Repeated shaking of an object.
Bringing movement to a halt.
Starting a stopped machine again.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-001.summary:

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-002.title: Put 5S into practice at a workbench
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-002.objective:
Distinguish the elements of 5S.
Explain how organizing relates to safety and quality.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
5S is not merely about making a workplace look tidy. It is a way to maintain a workplace where necessary items are easy to find, incorrect items are not used, and hazards and abnormalities are easier to notice.
Sorting means separating necessary and unnecessary items. However, do not discard drawings, inspection records, or entrusted items at your own discretion. Confirm the disposal criteria and who has authority. Setting in order means deciding where necessary items belong and how to return them so they can be retrieved without searching.
When cleaning, remove dirt while also looking for abnormalities such as leaks or damage. Cleaning inside machinery must follow the specified stopping and safety confirmation procedure. Maintaining cleanliness means sustaining the results of sorting, organizing, and cleaning. Discipline means understanding the agreed methods and following them as a habit.
An improvement will not last if a one-time cleanup cannot be maintained by the next person. Defining responsibility, when checks are performed, and whom to notify of abnormalities creates an activity that does not rely solely on individual effort.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
A workbench contains hex keys currently in use, a damaged hex key, and parts that have not been inspected, all mixed together.
1. Identify and segregate damaged tools by the prescribed method; confirm disposal with an authorized person.
2. Return usable tools to their designated locations and keep uninspected parts separate from accepted parts.
3. Clean under safe conditions and add tool condition to the end-of-shift checks.
Putting everything into one box does not prevent reuse of damaged tools or mixing in uninspected parts.

terms.meaning: Separating necessary from unnecessary items.
Arranging necessary items so they are easy to retrieve.
Maintaining a clean, orderly condition.
Following agreed actions as a habit.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-002.summary:
5S supports safety, quality, and efficiency.
Sorting and setting in order mean different things.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-003.title: Prevent tool and part mix-ups with three fixed conditions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-003.objective:
Explain fixed location, fixed item, and fixed quantity.
Distinguish a quantity shortage from an item in the wrong place.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
The three fixed conditions make the location, type, and quantity of items explicit. Fixed location specifies where to put them, fixed item specifies what to put there, and fixed quantity specifies how much to keep. Combining all three makes shortages and mixed items easier to detect.
Even if a tool outline marks its place, returning a different size of tool fails the fixed-item rule. Likewise, placing the correct parts on the correct shelf but stacking them beyond the limit can make retrieval difficult and lead to toppling or falling items.
More stock does not automatically mean greater reassurance. Set the amount according to the process requirement, replenishment timing, and storage method. Sharing how to report and replenish when stock falls below the lower limit makes the system easier to operate when staff change.
If you cannot read a location or item label, do not replenish parts based only on their appearance. Check the label and instructions; place unidentified items separately in the designated area and ask for advice.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
Shelf B-2 is specified to hold 12–24 parts for M8. A check finds 9 correct parts and 2 parts of another specification.
1. Identify the two different-specification parts as mixed items and handle them by the prescribed method.
2. Report that there are 9 correct parts, a shortage of 3 against the lower limit of 12.
3. Do not decide on the spot to fill the shelf to its maximum; follow the replenishment instruction.
Counting parts of another specification as stock gives an incorrect picture of the required quantity.

terms.meaning: Specifying where items are placed.
Specifying the type of item to place.
Specifying the quantity to place.
Adding what is missing.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-003.summary:
Check location, type, and quantity together.
Do not include different-specification parts in the same quantity.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-004.title: Check understanding and ability through OJT
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-004.objective:
Understand the roles of explanation, demonstration, practice, and checking.
Do not work independently with unresolved questions.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
When learning new work, understand why the steps follow that order rather than only memorizing the sequence. Before practice, confirm the pre-work inspection, prohibited actions, and response to abnormalities.
In OJT, the instructor explains and demonstrates, the learner practices within the specified scope, and the instructor checks the result. Having seen a task is not the same as being able to perform it safely alone. If an operation is unclear, stop and ask before attempting it.
After listening, explaining the procedure back in your own words helps reveal misunderstandings. In particular, do not rely on a vague acknowledgment when confirming values, units, part orientation, and stopping conditions.
Reading this material does not replace the training or qualifications required at the workplace. Confirm the work you may perform and the required training with the responsible person according to the equipment and working conditions.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
You have received an explanation of a tightening task, but do not understand how to check the tool’s setting.
1. Ask: “Please show me again where to check the setting and its unit.”
2. Watch the instructor demonstrate, then explain back where to check and how to read it.
3. Perform the specified practice, receive a check, and then confirm the scope of work you will handle.
Skipping the setting check can result in insufficient or excessive tightening.

terms.meaning: Performing a task to show someone how it is done.
A person who teaches the work method and checks performance.
The order and method for carrying out work.
Making sure the details are correct.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-004.summary:

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-005.title: Make hazards and countermeasures specific through KYT
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-005.objective:
Connect the cause of a hazard with its possible consequences.
Write an actionable behavior target.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
Hazard prediction should go beyond a general feeling that something is dangerous. Think specifically about what causes the danger, who may be affected, and what accident could occur. Looking separately at equipment, objects, people’s movements, and surrounding conditions helps reduce omissions.
The four stages of KYT involve identifying several hazards, selecting the most important ones, considering countermeasures, and deciding on the team’s actions. During discussion, share observations from people seeing the situation for the first time as well as experienced workers.
A countermeasure consisting only of “be careful” is insufficient. Decide what to check, when, and how. Do not try to resolve an equipment problem through worker attention alone; discuss improvements with the person responsible.
Review whether the chosen measures were carried out and whether they created another hazard. KYT is not a drill for approaching actual danger to test it. Use safe materials and explanations instead of recreating real hazards.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
A worker pushes a cart toward a corner. The load obstructs the forward view, and people are using the intersecting passage.
1. Write the hazard: “Continuing with an obstructed forward view could cause a collision with a pedestrian at the corner.”
2. Prioritize visibility and traffic flow issues, and check loading and transport methods with the responsible person.
3. Specify an actionable behavior, such as stopping and checking at the corner according to workplace rules.
Saying only “transport carefully” leaves the cause of the blocked forward view unresolved.

terms.meaning: Anticipating danger before an accident occurs.
A method to prevent or reduce a problem.
The route along which people or objects move.
A target expressed as an action to actually perform.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-005.summary:
Describe causes and consequences specifically.
Turn countermeasures into actionable behavior.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-006.title: Select protective equipment suitable for the task
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-006.objective:
Explain the hazards protective equipment guards against.
Understand when protective equipment itself can become a hazard.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
Protective equipment is used to shield the body from danger. Safety footwear, protective glasses, and gloves may differ in performance and purpose even when they share the same name. Use the type specified for your task and inspect it for damage, dirt, and proper fit before use.
Gloves protect hands during activities such as handling sharp material. However, they can become a source of danger in work where a rotating tool could catch them. Do not wear gloves while drilling with a drill press. Keep hands away from rotating parts and observe the prohibitions in the procedure.
Wearing protective glasses does not permit removal of a machine guard. Protective equipment must be used together with equipment safety measures and correct working methods. Check that its performance is appropriate for hazards such as flying particles, chemicals, or dust.
If the equipment does not fit, obscures your view, or is damaged, do not tolerate the problem and continue working; ask for replacement or adjustment. Do not substitute another person’s protective equipment without permission.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
The same worker handles sharp sheet material and drills holes with a drill press.
1. Check the hazards, specified protective equipment, and prohibitions for each task separately.
2. Use the specified suitable gloves when carrying sheet material, but do not wear gloves while drilling with the drill press. Keep hands away from rotating parts and change your equipment before switching tasks.
3. Check your equipment before moving to another process; if uncertain, ask the instructor before starting.
Protective equipment that is useful for one task is not necessarily safe for another.

terms.meaning: Items worn to protect the body from danger.
The body or clothing being pulled into a rotating component or similar object.
Small objects scattering into the surrounding area.
Attaching or putting something on in its specified position.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-006.summary:
Select protective equipment for the type of hazard.
Protective equipment does not replace guards or procedures.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-007.title: Assess risk and check again after countermeasures
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-007.objective:
Consider severity and likelihood of harm.
Check the risk remaining after countermeasures.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
When considering risk, look not only at whether a hazard exists but also at the severity of an accident, its likelihood, and opportunities for exposure. Use the workplace’s assessment method rather than deciding priorities solely by personal intuition.
First consider whether the hazard can be eliminated or reduced. If equipment or process changes are needed, consult the responsible person or department instead of modifying equipment without authorization. After implementation, check whether the measure works and whether a new hazard has been created.
Maintaining safety requires repeating a cycle of planning, implementation, evaluation, and necessary improvement. Inspection records and near misses provide information for the next improvement.
Do not assume that countermeasures completely eliminate the possibility of an accident. Machines can fail, misunderstandings can occur, and surroundings can change. Share the remaining hazards and maintain the ability to stop when something abnormal occurs.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
Oil occasionally leaks onto a passage. Cleaning has been the only response, but the floor becomes slippery again.
1. Confirm the slip-and-fall hazard and how often people pass through.
2. Apply workplace temporary measures, such as restricting entry, and request an investigation of the leak’s cause.
3. After repair or improvement, continue to check and record whether the leak recurs and the condition of the passage.
Cleaning is necessary, but the hazard will recur if the cause of the leak remains.

terms.meaning: A consideration of factors such as the severity and likelihood of harm from a hazard.
Judging a condition using specified criteria.
Considering a problem’s cause and making the condition better.
The level of risk that remains after countermeasures are applied.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-007.summary:

Do not omit checks after implementation.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-008.title: Read prohibition signs, warnings, and chemical labels
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-008.objective:
Distinguish prohibition from warning.
Do not use an unidentified container; check it first.

paragraphs.title: Principles and decisions
paragraphs.text:
Safety signs include those that prohibit actions, warn of a hazard, and indicate locations or equipment needed in an emergency. Do not only memorize the picture; consider what action is required at that location.
“No entry” does not mean you may enter if you are careful. An electric-shock warning indicates the presence of an electrical hazard. Follow the sign and confirm the equipment procedure and your authorization to enter the area.
For chemicals, check the container label and safety data sheet. Hazards such as ignition, corrosion, and health effects differ by substance. Do not identify contents solely by color or smell, or use liquid from an unlabeled container.
Check the locations and routes to fire extinguishers, AEDs, and evacuation areas during normal conditions instead of starting to search in an emergency. If an escape route is obstructed, request improvement according to workplace rules.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
While preparing a cleaning operation, you find a container with an unreadable label next to a familiar cleaning liquid.
1. Do not use the container with the unreadable label, mix its contents, or transfer them to another container.
2. Tell the responsible person where it is stored and its condition, and confirm the contents and correct handling.
3. For a substance authorized for use, check the label, safety data sheet, and work procedure.
Similar containers placed beside one another do not prove that their contents are identical.

terms.meaning: An action that must not be performed.
A sign indicating the presence of a dangerous or harmful condition.
Deterioration of a material through chemical or similar action.
A route taken to move away from danger.

safety: Do not try to identify an unknown liquid by touching or smelling it.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-008.summary:

Check an unreadable label before use.

mfg1-electrical-l001.title: Choose tools that match the wire and terminal
mfg1-electrical-l001.objective:
Distinguish conductor cross-sectional area from diameter
Check the combination of wire, terminal, and tool

paragraphs.title: Checks before processing
paragraphs.text:
A terminal may fit the screw on a terminal block but still be unsuitable for the wire size. Check the wire type, conductor size, terminal application range, and specified crimping tool separately. Do not choose the combination by appearance alone.
The diameter of a solid conductor in mm and the cross-sectional area of a stranded conductor in mm² are different quantities. A wire marked 1.25 mm² does not automatically match a blade marked for a 1.25 mm diameter. Check the tool application table for the correct setting.

paragraphs.title: Stripping and crimping
paragraphs.text:
A wire stripper removes insulation. A cut that is too deep can damage the conductor; one that is too shallow can leave insulation behind. After stripping, compare cut strands, damage, and strip length with the work standard.
Crimping is not simply crushing a terminal with pliers. Use the specified terminal and compatible tool, then check the result by the prescribed method. A terminal being attached does not by itself make the connection acceptable.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
A tool displaying only solid-wire diameters is supplied for work using 1.25 mm² stranded wire.
1. Check the wire specification for conductor type and cross-sectional area.
2. Check the tool application table. If compatibility remains unclear, ask the responsible person before starting.
3. Make a trial connection with the approved combination and check strip length, conductor damage, and crimp condition against the standard.
Similar numbers do not justify the same tool setting when units and application conditions differ.

terms.meaning: The covering that protects a conductor.
An individual fine wire that forms part of a stranded conductor.
A terminal attached to wire by compression with a tool.
The area of a cross section.

Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.

Write down whether the wire is solid or stranded and which unit its marking uses.

Explain that mm and mm² describe different quantities.
Do not fill unknown compatibility conditions with guesses.
safety: Do not process energized wires. Follow workplace procedures and your assigned responsibilities for isolating the supply and verifying absence of voltage.
Do not force an incompatible terminal or tool.
mfg1-electrical-l001.summary:
Distinguish mm from mm².
Check wire, terminal, and crimping tool as one combination.

mfg1-electrical-l002.title: Understand soldering through the condition of the joint
mfg1-electrical-l002.objective:
Explain why the joint must be heated
Explain how movement before cooling can cause defects

paragraphs.title: Where to apply heat
paragraphs.text:
In soldering, heat the metal joint appropriately so solder can spread over the joining surfaces. Simply placing a large blob melted on the iron tip onto a cold joint may fail to produce the required connection.
Before work, check the materials, tip, temperature setting, solder, and flux against the work standard. Leaded and lead-free solder differ in their properties. Do not mix materials or carry over settings from another job without checking.

paragraphs.title: From heating to cooling
paragraphs.text:
Hold the joint still, heat it by the specified method, and supply solder. Both insufficient heating and excessively prolonged heating can affect quality. Do not memorize one universal time or temperature; follow the component requirements and work standard.
Moving a component or wire while solder is solidifying can disturb the joint. After cooling, inspect solder spread, insufficient solder, and bridging to adjacent areas. Use the specified inspection for items that appearance alone cannot establish.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
Someone is about to pull a wire to correct its position immediately after soldering it to a terminal.
1. Do not move a joint while it is solidifying.
2. After cooling, compare its position and condition with the inspection criteria.
3. If it is nonconforming, check the approved rework procedure rather than bending it into place and shipping it.
Preserving the joint and following the prescribed disposition matter more than correcting position quickly.

terms.meaning: The part where materials are joined.
The tendency of molten solder to spread over a joining surface.
Reducing temperature.
A condition in which the required amount of solder is missing.

mfg1-electrical-l002.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.
Explain the sequence that prevents defects
Explain cleaning, securing, heating, solder supply, cooling, and inspection in order.
Describe what can happen if position is corrected during cooling.
Explain why a single temperature setting cannot be assigned to every job.
Explain why the joint itself is heated.
Check differences in materials, components, and standards.
safety: Do not touch the iron tip or metal immediately after soldering. Use an iron stand.
Follow workplace procedures and product information for ventilation, local exhaust, and handling cleaning agents.
mfg1-electrical-l002.summary:
Check joint temperature and the material combination.
Keep the joint still until it has cooled sufficiently.

mfg1-electrical-l003.title: Use the right caliper surfaces and a consistent reading method
mfg1-electrical-l003.objective:
Choose the measuring surfaces for outside, inside, and depth measurements
Confirm the smallest readable increment and record the measurement

paragraphs.title: Choose the measuring surfaces
paragraphs.text:
Use outside jaws for external dimensions, inside jaws for internal dimensions such as holes, and the depth bar for depth. The reference surface changes even when the same caliper is used. Identify the measurement location on the drawing before measuring.
Dirt and chips on measuring surfaces affect the result. Clean the surfaces and check instrument condition and zero. Avoid applying the jaws at an angle or using excessive clamping force.

paragraphs.title: Main scale and vernier
paragraphs.text:
For a vernier caliper, add the fractional value read from the vernier to the main-scale reading. Scale arrangements vary by model, so check the smallest readable increment of the actual instrument first. Display digits alone do not establish equal accuracy.
Always include the unit and record the part and measurement location. If a result is close to a specification limit, do not round it arbitrarily to obtain a pass; check the prescribed decision method.

paragraphs.title: Formulae and units
paragraphs.text: Measurement = main-scale reading + vernier fraction

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
On a caliper with a 0.05 mm smallest readable increment, the main-scale integer part is 22 mm and the vernier alignment indicates 0.35 mm.
1. Record the main-scale integer part as 22 mm.
2. Add the fractional vernier reading of 0.35 mm.
3. Record 22 + 0.35 = 22.35 mm, including the unit.
The reading is 22.35 mm. Acceptance cannot be decided from that value alone; check the drawing tolerance and decision procedure.

terms.meaning: The main reference scale.
Lines or indications used to read a quantity.
The outside diameter.
The surface where the instrument contacts the object.

Explain that acceptance requires a permitted range.
safety: Do not place calipers against rotating or moving objects.

mfg1-electrical-l003.summary:
Use the part of the instrument suited to the measurement location.
Keep zero checks, smallest readable increment, and contact method consistent.

mfg1-electrical-l004.title: Do not overlook the 0.5 mm mark on a micrometer
mfg1-electrical-l004.objective:
Combine sleeve and thimble readings
Explain the purpose of consistent measuring force

paragraphs.title: Preparation and measuring force
paragraphs.text:
An outside micrometer measures a dimension by holding the object between the anvil and spindle. Clean the measuring faces and check range and zero before use. Outside, inside, and depth micrometers are different types; the general name alone does not determine the application.
For final contact, use the constant-force device according to the instructions for that model. Excessive tightening can deform the object or instrument, making results inconsistent even for the same object.

paragraphs.title: Add the two readings
paragraphs.text:
On a common scale-type micrometer with a 0.01 mm smallest readable increment, check the sleeve marks for both 1 mm and 0.5 mm, then the thimble fraction. Always check whether the 0.5 mm line is visible.
A thimble showing 12 does not necessarily mean the full measurement is 0.12 mm. Add 0.12 mm to the sleeve value. If the instrument has a different scale arrangement, use its own reading method.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
The sleeve shows 6 mm and the following 0.5 mm line. The thimble, graduated in 0.01 mm increments, indicates 24.
1. Read the sleeve as 6.5 mm.
2. Read the thimble as 24 × 0.01 = 0.24 mm.
3. Calculate 6.5 + 0.24 = 6.74 mm.
The result is 6.74 mm. Missing the 0.5 mm line produces 6.24 mm, an error of 0.50 mm.

terms.meaning: The force with which measuring faces press on the object.
A mechanism for keeping measuring force consistent.
The line used as a reference when reading a scale.
The fractional value smaller than the integer part.

mfg1-electrical-l004.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.

Calculate the value for a 9.0 mm sleeve reading and thimble 31.
Calculate the value for a 9.5 mm sleeve reading and the same thimble 31.
Explain the difference and why measuring force must be consistent.
Distinguish 9.31 mm from 9.81 mm.
Do not describe excessive tightening as a way to improve accuracy.
safety: Do not measure a rotating shaft.
Do not use a measuring instrument as a clamp.
mfg1-electrical-l004.summary:
Do not miss the 0.5 mm line.
Clean measuring faces and consistent force support repeatable results.

mfg1-electrical-l005.title: Decide the quantity and connection before using a multimeter
mfg1-electrical-l005.objective:
Explain different connections for voltage, current, and resistance
Check terminals, function, and range before measurement

paragraphs.title: Decide what to measure
paragraphs.text:
Voltage is the potential difference between two points, so connect a voltmeter in parallel across those points. Current is the quantity flowing through a branch, so insert an ammeter in series in that branch. Placing a meter set to current across a supply can cause a short circuit or instrument damage.
An instrument has specified applications, input terminals, maximum inputs, and safety ratings. A higher range alone does not make measurement safe on every installation. Before measuring real equipment, check required qualifications and training, equipment procedures, and instrument suitability.

paragraphs.title: Resistance measurement and checks after use
paragraphs.text:
Resistance measurement uses the instrument’s internal source, so do not perform it on an energized circuit. Besides turning power off, follow prescribed procedures for residual charge and isolate the component from the circuit where required.
After measurement, check that a lead has not been left in the current input terminal. Return the instrument to the workplace’s prescribed state to prevent an accident when the next person measures voltage. Analog resistance ranges also require zero adjustment for each range.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
Before measuring voltage on a low-voltage DC training circuit, you notice the red lead is connected to the current input terminal.
1. Do not connect to the circuit yet.
2. Follow the manual to check the voltage input terminal, DC voltage function, and appropriate range.
3. After the instructor’s check, connect in parallel across the specified two points.
Check quantity, terminal, function, range, and connection together.

terms.meaning: A connection in which both ends connect to the same two points.
A connection in which parts are placed consecutively in the same path.
Charge that remains after the supply is switched off.
The distinction between positive and negative, for example.

mfg1-electrical-l005.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.
Write a verbal pre-measurement check
Organize the conditions for voltage, current, and resistance measurement in three columns.
Write checks for terminals, function, range, and safety rating.
Explain the response to finding a lead left in a current terminal.
Do not confuse parallel with series.
Check both absence of power and handling of residual charge for resistance measurement.
safety: Understanding this lesson alone does not authorize live work. Follow assigned responsibilities, training, and procedures for equipment measurement.
Do not connect a current range directly across a supply.
mfg1-electrical-l005.summary:
Voltage: parallel. Current: series.
Measure resistance only without power and after necessary precautions.

mfg1-electrical-l006.title: Use Ohm’s law with the correct units
mfg1-electrical-l006.objective:
Calculate the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance
Distinguish mA from A

paragraphs.title: The relationship between three quantities
paragraphs.text:
For a resistor obeying Ohm’s law at constant temperature, voltage V, current I, and resistance R satisfy V = I × R. The units used here are V, A, and Ω. Convert to consistent units before substituting numbers into the formula.
1 A is 1000 mA and 1 kΩ is 1000 Ω. For example, 8 mA is 0.008 A. Substituting the numeric mA value as though it were A gives a result different by a factor of 1000.

paragraphs.title: Connect a calculation to practical decisions
paragraphs.text:
For the same resistance, increasing the applied voltage increases current. Real equipment can contain components other than resistors and can change with temperature, so do not judge an entire installation from this simple formula alone.
Calculation is one way to check ratings and specifications. Finding the current does not establish whether a component can withstand the heating or whether the supply has enough capacity. Check those separately.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
For a calculation exercise, consider an ideal 2.0 kΩ resistor connected to a 12 V DC supply.
1. Convert 2.0 kΩ to 2000 Ω.
2. I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 2000 = 0.006 A.
3. Convert 0.006 A to 6 mA.
The ideal current is 6 mA. Before an actual connection, also check resistor and supply ratings.

terms.meaning: The electric potential difference between two points.
The magnitude of charge flow.
A quantity expressing opposition to current flow.
A specified value defining conditions of use.

mfg1-electrical-l006.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.
Convert units and calculate different conditions
Find current in A and mA for an ideal 3.0 kΩ resistor at 9 V.
Find voltage for an ideal 1.5 kΩ resistor carrying 6 mA.
List rating checks needed in addition to the calculated result.
Obtain 0.003 A = 3 mA.
Obtain 0.006 × 1500 = 9 V.
safety: Do not treat calculation exercise values as instructions for connecting real equipment.
Do not short-circuit a supply.
mfg1-electrical-l006.summary:
Convert units to A, Ω, and other required units before substitution.
Calculation and rating checks are separate checks.

mfg1-electrical-l007.title: Read period and amplitude on an oscilloscope
mfg1-electrical-l007.objective:
Distinguish vertical-axis and horizontal-axis units
Calculate frequency from period

paragraphs.title: What one division represents
paragraphs.text:
An oscilloscope displays how a signal such as voltage changes with time. Vertical V/div is voltage per division; horizontal s/div is time per division. A number of divisions alone does not determine voltage or time.
The voltage difference between a peak and trough in the vertical direction is the peak-to-peak value. If the waveform is symmetric about zero, amplitude from zero to the peak is half that value. Do not simply halve an offset waveform without checking the zero reference.

paragraphs.title: Time for the same condition to repeat
paragraphs.text:
A period is the time until a waveform returns to the same state. For example, read from one zero crossing to the next crossing in the same direction. Peak to trough is normally not one full period.
Frequency f is found from f = 1/T. Convert T to seconds before calculating to obtain Hz. Do not use a numeric millisecond value as if it were seconds.

paragraphs.title: Formulae and units
paragraphs.text:
T = time-axis setting × divisions per period
f = 1 / T
10 ms = 0.010 s

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
A training waveform uses 2 ms/div and spans 5 div per period. It is centered on zero, with a peak-to-trough span of 4 div at 1 V/div.
1. T = 2 × 5 = 10 ms = 0.010 s.
2. f = 1 ÷ 0.010 = 100 Hz.
3. Peak-to-trough voltage is 4 V; symmetry about zero gives a 2 V amplitude.
Period: 10 ms; frequency: 100 Hz; peak-to-peak voltage: 4 V; amplitude: 2 V.

terms.meaning: The time until the same state repeats.
The number of repetitions per second.
The magnitude of excursion from a reference.
A shape representing change over time.

mfg1-electrical-l007.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.
Read after changing the time-axis setting
Find period and frequency for 1 ms/div and a 4-div period.
Find the divisions for the same period after changing to 0.5 ms/div.
Explain why peak to trough is not counted as one period.
Obtain 4 ms = 0.004 s and 250 Hz.
Obtain 8 div and explain that the signal’s period itself has not changed.
safety: Do not connect to real equipment without checking the probe grounding arrangement.
Check input ratings, probe attenuation, and the measurement procedure.
mfg1-electrical-l007.summary:
Multiply divisions by the axis setting to obtain a quantity.
Convert period to seconds before taking its reciprocal.

mfg1-electrical-l008.title: Prevent escape of assembly defects and record findings
mfg1-electrical-l008.objective:
Explain differences between visual, dimensional, and functional inspection
Identify and report nonconforming products

paragraphs.title: Each inspection has a different purpose
paragraphs.text:
Visual inspection checks items such as missing parts, mounting direction, damage, and solder bridges against criteria. Dimensional inspection measures lengths and spacing at specified locations. Functional inspection checks whether required behavior occurs for a given input. Passing one does not justify omitting the others.
Inspections of components, populated boards, and finished products have different objects and check items. Match part number, revision, serial number, and inspection items to the inspection sheet before starting. Do not use criteria for a similar-looking but different product.

paragraphs.title: What to do after finding a problem
paragraphs.text:
When a nonconformity is found, identify the product and hold or segregate it under workplace procedures so it cannot mix with acceptable products. Record location, observed facts, quantity, and lot information. Do not record an unconfirmed guess as an established cause.
Rework and reinspection follow decisions by authorized people and approved methods. Someone outside the assigned role should not add energization or high-voltage testing to investigate. Records should allow later tracing of which product was judged against which criteria.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text:
During visual inspection of a board, solder appears to connect adjacent terminals, but the outer box bears an inspected label.
1. Do not accept solely on the label; check product identification and inspection history.
2. Hold the product according to procedure and record the location and condition.
3. Report to the responsible person and obtain directions for approved inspection, rework, and re-evaluation.
Even when the inspection label conflicts with the observed condition, prevent escape and maintain traceable records.

terms.meaning: Inspection comparing externally observable condition with criteria.
Failure to meet a requirement or criterion.
Separating and controlling items so they cannot mix.
Following history or a route for confirmation.

mfg1-electrical-l008.activity:
Explain the decision in the example in your own words, then write three items to check against the workplace work standard.
Write an inspection-hold report
Create fields for part number, serial number, finding location, observed facts, and held quantity.
Report a suspected solder bridge without asserting a cause.
Explain the difference between unauthorized rework and approved reinspection.
Separate facts from assumptions.
Include prevention of mixing and information needed for tracing.
safety: Safety and withstand-voltage tests must use approved equipment, procedures, and assigned personnel.
Do not energize a suspected defective product without authorization.
mfg1-electrical-l008.summary:
A pass in one inspection item does not replace another inspection.
Keep product identification and factual records consistent.

mfg1-surface-lesson-001.title: Check hazards and protective equipment before surface-treatment work
mfg1-surface-lesson-001.objective:
Distinguish chemical hazards from rotating-machine hazards.
Explain the relationship between labels, procedures and protective equipment.

paragraphs.title: A job name alone does not determine safety
paragraphs.text:
Even in the same plating workplace, taking a chemical sample and using a rotating tool involve different hazards. First check what could splash or fly out, which parts must not be touched, and where to move in an emergency. Familiarity with a task does not mean the same judgement remains valid after materials or equipment change.
Do not rely on protective equipment alone; prioritize measures that remove hazards. Check that guards, local exhaust ventilation and work zones are functioning properly, then use the specified protective equipment.

paragraphs.title: Connect chemical labels with the work procedure
paragraphs.text:
A container label identifies hazards as well as the chemical name. A corrosive label calls for attention not only to skin and eye contact but also to effects on containers and surrounding materials. Before use, check the safety data sheet (SDS) and workplace procedure, and select the specified glove material and eye or face protection.
Do not use a container with an unreadable label or unknown contents. Do not guess its contents from appearance or smell. Report the container identification, location and time found, and keep it out of use until the responsible person has checked it.

paragraphs.title: Prevent entanglement
paragraphs.text:
Gloves that protect against chemicals can become an entanglement hazard near rotating parts. Do not memorize “gloves always make work safe”; check the procedure and prohibitions for each machine. Jewellery, loose sleeves and untied hair also require attention.
Stopping equipment is not the same as establishing a safe condition for work. For inspection, replacement or cleaning, a trained person must follow the prescribed process to prevent restarting and control stored energy.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: A worker who has taken a chemical sample is about to grind a jig on a nearby rotating tool while still wearing the same gloves. First check the machine work standard and prohibitions. Gloves required for sampling cannot automatically be considered suitable for another task. If you have not been trained for the task, ask the designated worker and do not start it yourself.

terms.meaning: Equipment worn to protect the body from hazards.
Clothing or the body being drawn into rotating parts.
A property that can damage skin, metals or other materials.

terms.reading: さぎょうひょうじゅん
terms.meaning: The prescribed work method and control conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-001.activity:
Choose one task you perform and explain its splash, contact and entanglement hazards separately.
Write three pieces of information to report when you find an unreadable container label.
safety: Do not mix unidentified chemicals or smell them directly.
This material does not replace qualifications, practical training or equipment-specific work authorization.
mfg1-surface-lesson-001.summary:
Select protective equipment for each task.
Check chemical labels and the SDS, and the machine work standard.
If a hazard is unclear, check before starting.

mfg1-surface-lesson-002.title: Read pH changes and record measurement results
mfg1-surface-lesson-002.objective:
Explain the relationship between pH and hydrogen-ion concentration.
Distinguish measured values from process acceptance limits.

paragraphs.title: A difference in numbers and a difference in concentration
paragraphs.text:
pH indicates acidity or alkalinity. In a dilute aqueous solution, pH can be approximated as the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration expressed in mol/L. When pH decreases by 1, hydrogen-ion concentration increases by approximately ten times.
The difference between pH 4 and pH 5 does not mean simply “one more unit of acid.” Nor can pH alone determine all component concentrations or the hazards of a liquid. Other conditions, including concentration, temperature and mixtures, must also be considered.

paragraphs.title: Choose the measurement method
paragraphs.text:
Test paper is useful for quickly checking an approximate range. Where precise control is required, use the specified pH meter. Check the colour-to-value relationship for the particular product; not all test papers use the same colours.
With a pH meter, check instrument inspection and calibration, electrode condition, sample temperature and whether the reading has stabilized. Different sampling locations or measurement times can change the meaning of a comparison. Use and record the measurement conditions prescribed by the workplace.

paragraphs.title: Do not adjust the bath without authorization
paragraphs.text:
The control range depends on the purpose of the process. A value close to neutral is not necessarily desirable. If a value is outside the range, check the measurement conditions, record the affected lot and time, and report to the responsible person.
Mixing acids and alkalis can cause heat generation and splashing. Do not add chemicals simply to restore a number; follow the approved adjustment procedure.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: Assume a training-only control range of pH 4.6–5.0. A morning reading of 4.8 is within it, but a later reading of 4.3 is outside it. Do not dismiss the change from 4.8 to 4.3 as too small to matter. Check calibration and sample conditions, then report the sampling time, liquid temperature and bath identification. This range is illustrative, not an actual bath setting.

terms.meaning: An acidic property related to hydrogen ions.
The concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution.
Checking an instrument indication against a standard.
The range of values permitted for a process.

mfg1-surface-lesson-002.activity:
Explain the ratio of hydrogen-ion concentrations at pH 3 and pH 5.
List three checks to make when a measurement is unstable.
safety: Do not add or mix chemicals on the learner’s judgement alone.
A simple concentration approximation has limits for concentrated or unusual solutions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-002.summary:
A pH difference of 1 corresponds to approximately a tenfold difference in hydrogen-ion concentration.
Record measurement conditions and calibration status.
Judge results against the process control range.

mfg1-surface-lesson-003.title: Evaluate film thickness at each location, not only the average
mfg1-surface-lesson-003.objective:
Avoid overlooking locally thin or thick areas.
Check a measurement method suitable for the substrate and film.

paragraphs.title: Why film thickness matters
paragraphs.text:
A film affects not only appearance but also corrosion resistance and electrical properties. Similar appearance does not guarantee the same thickness. Check the specified measurement positions, method and acceptance range in the work standard.
Passing an entire item after measuring one location may overlook differences at edges or recesses. Measure the specified locations and retain the maximum and minimum values together with their positions. An average alone can conceal a local shortfall.

paragraphs.title: Choose a method for the material combination
paragraphs.text:
X-ray fluorescence, magnetic methods, eddy-current methods and cross-sectional observation use different principles. Applicability depends on the substrate, film material, layer structure and shape. Do not assume the same instrument works simply because both items are metal.
Check the instrument with suitable standards or reference samples, and consider the effects of curvature and edges. Follow the instrument specification and approved measurement procedure. At this stage, do not memorize a universal application range from the instrument category alone.

paragraphs.title: Separate product nonconformity from measurement problems
paragraphs.text:
If a result is outside the range, identify and separate the item from acceptable products, check measurement conditions and instrument status, and report it. Do not move the measurement location or delete unfavourable results to make the outcome look better.
Methods that cut a cross-section or dissolve the film alter the sample. Do not process goods intended for shipment without authorization; use samples designated in the inspection plan.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: For practice, assume an allowed thickness of 8–12 μm. Three specified points give 7, 10 and 13 μm. The average is (7+10+13)/3 = 10 μm, but two points are outside the range. Do not pass the item on the average alone; record each location and value. The 8–12 μm range is a teaching assumption, not a recommended process setting.

terms.meaning: The thickness of a coating or film.
The underlying material on which a film is formed.
Inspection that does not damage the item.
An item that does not meet specified requirements.

mfg1-surface-lesson-003.activity:
Identify the minimum, maximum and out-of-range positions in the example.
Explain what to check before reusing the same instrument after the substrate changes.
safety: Use equipment involving X-rays or other controlled sources under the prescribed training and management procedures.
Do not cut or chemically process an item for inspection without authorization.
mfg1-surface-lesson-003.summary:
Retain measurement positions and individual readings.
An acceptable average does not mean every point is acceptable.
Check the method for the substrate and film combination.

mfg1-surface-lesson-004.title: Understand corrosion through small holes and dissimilar-metal contact
mfg1-surface-lesson-004.objective:
Explain the relationship between film defects and corrosion.
Organize the conditions involved in dissimilar-metal contact.

paragraphs.title: A film does not justify complete confidence
paragraphs.text:
Even a surface-treated item can be affected by its environment through scratches or tiny holes. A pinhole is a very small hole at the surface. Causes may lie in the film, substrate or preceding process, so record precisely where it is and what it looks like.
A change visible only in one small area may accompany corrosion spreading beneath the film. Polishing away the visible mark does not establish the cause or justify acceptance.

paragraphs.title: Consider contact together with the presence of liquid
paragraphs.text:
When metals with different properties contact each other and an electrolyte such as an aqueous solution is involved, electrochemical action can accelerate corrosion of one metal. Check not only metal names but also contact conditions, liquid, dirt, scratches and storage conditions.
The tendency to ionize helps explain the mechanism, but actual corrosion also depends on films, environment and relative areas. Do not infer corrosion rates in every environment from a table alone.

paragraphs.title: Feed observations back into the process
paragraphs.text:
If discolouration or corrosion repeatedly appears at the same location, investigate possible relationships with jig contact, residual rinse water or foreign matter introduced during packaging. Avoid deciding on one cause prematurely; compare lot numbers, processing dates, storage locations and affected areas.
Identify and hold products suspected of nonconformity. Rework methods and feasibility depend on material, dimensions and required quality. Workers must not independently grind the item or return it to a chemical bath.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: Before shipment, corrosion is found only where a metal fragment was touching the product. Instead of immediately concluding that the film was too thin, examine the fragment, moisture, packaging and other products in the same lot. Separate the product from acceptable goods, mark the contact position on a sketch, and pass the information to quality staff.

terms.meaning: Deterioration or damage caused by a material reacting with its environment.
Preventing corrosion.
Metals of different types.
A substance that carries electrical charge through ions in a solution or similar medium.

mfg1-surface-lesson-004.activity:
List four kinds of workplace information to check when considering contact corrosion.
Explain why merely polishing away the visible mark does not solve the problem.
safety: Do not touch an unidentified liquid to inspect it.
Rework nonconforming items only under approved instructions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-004.summary:
Pinholes can provide an entry point for corrosion beneath a film.
Check contact, electrolyte and environment together.
Do not decide a cause or rework method from appearance alone.

mfg1-surface-lesson-005.title: Distinguish the anode and cathode in electroplating
mfg1-surface-lesson-005.objective:
Explain where the workpiece is placed in electroplating.
Do not confuse soluble and insoluble anodes.

paragraphs.title: The power supply and two electrodes
paragraphs.text:
In ordinary direct-current electroplating, the workpiece receiving the film is on the cathode side. Metal ions in the solution receive electrons and appear as metal on its surface. A reaction that receives electrons is called reduction.
Oxidation occurs at the anode. In a process with a soluble metal anode, anode metal enters the solution as ions. However, anodes do not dissolve in the same way in every plating process.

paragraphs.title: The bath and jig are part of the process
paragraphs.text:
Placing the item on the correct side is not sufficient. Jig contact, which provides the current path, the workpiece surface condition and bath control conditions also matter. Poor contact may prevent the intended current from reaching the item.
The power-supply display cannot fully describe the condition at the workpiece surface. Before starting, check the specified wiring, jigs and racking arrangement, then monitor the prescribed items during processing.

paragraphs.title: Differences from other surface treatments
paragraphs.text:
Electroless plating does not pass current from an external supply to the workpiece in the same way as ordinary electroplating. The workpiece also plays a different electrode role in anodizing. Confirm the process name before applying a memorized polarity to another process.
A teaching diagram explains reactions; it is not permission to disconnect or reverse actual equipment wiring. Ask authorized personnel to make changes to electrical equipment.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: In a training diagram, consider a solution containing copper ions and a soluble copper anode. Pair the anode reaction Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ with the workpiece-side reaction Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. This explains the basic reactions; it does not mean every bath composition or installation uses the same copper anode.

terms.meaning: The electrode at which oxidation occurs.
The electrode at which reduction occurs.
The appearance of a solid from components in a solution or another phase.
A reaction in which electrons are received.

mfg1-surface-lesson-005.activity:
In the copper example, explain which side releases electrons and which receives them.
Explain why the external-supply polarity description cannot be directly applied to electroless plating.
safety: Do not touch energized jigs or wiring.
Only authorized personnel may change wiring or repair power supplies.
mfg1-surface-lesson-005.summary:
In ordinary electroplating, the workpiece is the cathode.
Metal ions receive electrons and deposit as metal.
Anode material and reactions vary with the process.

mfg1-surface-lesson-006.title: Relate current density and workpiece shape to thickness variation
mfg1-surface-lesson-006.objective:
Distinguish current from current density.
Explain how shape can produce an uneven film.

paragraphs.title: Consider current relative to area
paragraphs.text:
With the same current, changing the area being treated changes the current per unit area. Current density describes how much current flows per unit area. Use consistent units, such as A and dm², when calculating it.
The treated area is not necessarily just the projected area of one face. Confirm the calculation assumptions and process rules for both faces, edges, hole interiors and masked areas that are not treated.

paragraphs.title: The average and the local distribution
paragraphs.text:
Calculating average current density does not mean every part of the surface has that value. Current distribution can differ between edges or projections and recesses, producing thickness differences.
Areas where current concentrates generally tend to become thicker, while areas less accessible to current tend to become thinner. Bath properties, arrangement and agitation also affect the result, so shape alone does not determine the final thickness.

paragraphs.title: Increasing a value is not always an improvement
paragraphs.text:
More current does not necessarily improve the process. Exceeding the specified conditions can impair appearance or stable deposition. Do not change control settings, rack loading or treated area without authorization.
If thickness varies, record measurements by location, the racking arrangement and process conditions, then report them. Responsible staff evaluate and decide countermeasures such as arrangement changes or auxiliary jigs.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: For calculation practice, a treated area of 2.4 dm² with a current of 7.2 A gives an average current density of 7.2 ÷ 2.4 = 3.0 A/dm². If only the area doubles to 4.8 dm² while current stays the same, it becomes 1.5 A/dm². These are practice figures, not recommended conditions for an actual bath.

terms.meaning: Current per unit area.
The distance between the anode and cathode.
A part that projects beyond its surroundings.
The surface area subject to treatment.

mfg1-surface-lesson-006.activity:
Use 100 cm² = 1 dm² to convert 240 cm² to dm².
Explain why edges and recesses can have different thicknesses despite the same overall average current density.
safety: Do not enter teaching-example values directly into actual equipment.
Obtain authorization before changing rack loading, power conditions or jig arrangement.
mfg1-surface-lesson-006.summary:
Average current density equals current divided by area.
Local distribution differs from the average.
Relate shape and process conditions to thickness measurements.

mfg1-surface-lesson-007.title: Anodizing forms an oxide film from the substrate
mfg1-surface-lesson-007.objective:
Explain the difference between plating and anodizing.
Understand the purpose of pretreatment and film structure.

paragraphs.title: Different from depositing another metal
paragraphs.text:
Aluminium anodizing forms an oxide film at the substrate surface. Distinguish it from ordinary electroplating that deposits another metal on the item. In anodizing, the aluminium workpiece is treated on the anode side.
Aluminium naturally forms a thin oxide film, but it is not necessarily sufficient for every service environment. A controlled process forms a film suited to required corrosion resistance, wear resistance and appearance.

paragraphs.title: The pretreatment condition carries into the next process
paragraphs.text:
Residual oil and foreign matter make uniform treatment difficult. Preliminary finishing, degreasing, etching and desmutting have different purposes; do not treat them as identical cleaning steps.
Process sequence, solution, temperature and time depend on material and required quality. Do not try to conceal a pretreatment problem in a later process. Identify affected items when the issue is discovered and retain their processing history.

paragraphs.title: Understand pores and the barrier layer conceptually
paragraphs.text:
A typical porous film includes a region with fine pores and a dense barrier layer next to the substrate. Some colouring methods use the pores, but colouring and corrosion-resistance evaluation are not the same.
Post-treatments such as sealing are selected for the required properties. Do not judge solely that an attractive colour is acceptable or that thicker is always better; evaluate the specified inspection items.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: A newcomer describes an anodized item as having “a silver-coloured metal plated on top.” The instructor clarifies that this process forms an oxide film from the aluminium surface itself. Mark the workpiece on the anode side in the process diagram, then compare it with the cathode-side workpiece in electroplating.

terms.meaning: A process that uses the workpiece as the anode to form an oxide film.
A surface film made of oxide.
Treatment to close pores in a film.
Removing oil from the surface.

mfg1-surface-lesson-007.activity:
Explain the workpiece electrode in electroplating and anodizing respectively.
Give reasons why colour alone cannot establish film quality.
safety: Chemical resistance depends on conditions; do not generalize that an oxide film resists every chemical.
Chemical preparation and process-setting changes require approved procedures and training.
mfg1-surface-lesson-007.summary:
The workpiece is the anode and forms an oxide film.
Film formation differs from plating.
Inspect appearance, thickness and required properties separately.

mfg1-surface-lesson-008.title: Control scratches and heat between buffing stages
mfg1-surface-lesson-008.objective:
Explain why preceding-stage scratches should be addressed before moving on.
Relate burning and uneven finish to work conditions.

paragraphs.title: Prepare the surface before producing gloss
paragraphs.text:
Buffing uses a buff and polishing compound to finish a surface. Its purposes include removing scratches or burrs and producing uniform appearance, not just final gloss. An acceptable appearance differs between mirror finish and a low-gloss finish.
Residual oil or foreign matter can disrupt process stability. Check the surface during pretreatment and progress from reducing coarse scratches to finishing. Changing to fine finishing conditions does not automatically remove deep scratches.

paragraphs.title: Pressure and heat
paragraphs.text:
Excessive pressure increases frictional heat and can cause discolouration called burning or defects from removing too much material at corners. Applying more force to finish faster does not necessarily produce a better result.
Keep buff condition, compound, rotation conditions and feed method consistent, then inspect the finish. Use specified rotation speed and compound suitable for the material and machine; this lesson does not establish a universal setting.

paragraphs.title: Record causes of unevenness and scratches
paragraphs.text:
When unevenness appears, organize information on changed conditions such as contact angle, force, feed and uneven buff wear. Repeatedly polishing harder without investigation can damage dimensions or corner shapes.
After buffing, inspect appearance under specified lighting and viewing direction, and check dimensions or other properties where required. Do not remove an unacceptable amount of material merely to improve appearance. Follow prescribed safety procedures for equipment servicing and buff replacement.

paragraphs.title: Workplace example
paragraphs.text: A single deep scratch remains after finishing. Instead of pressing harder to remove it, check whether a scratch that should have been addressed in the preceding stage remains. Identify the item, record the scratch location and preceding-stage conditions, and consult the instructor. Decide whether re-buffing is possible only after checking dimensions and required quality.

terms.meaning: Finishing a surface with a buff and polishing compound.
Discolouration caused by frictional heat or similar heating.
An initial polishing stage that removes larger scratches.
A finish with mirror-like gloss.

mfg1-surface-lesson-008.activity:
List the conditions to check for burning and for unevenness separately.
Explain what to check before continuing to polish a deep scratch with greater force.
safety: Follow machine-specific procedures to prevent clothing, hair or gloves from being drawn into rotating parts.
Do not independently replace, clean or adjust a buff while it is rotating.
mfg1-surface-lesson-008.summary:
Check preceding-stage scratches before finishing.
Excessive pressure can cause heat and shape defects.
Record specified conditions and observations to investigate causes.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-009.title: Consider quality from the user’s requirements
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-009.objective: Distinguish design, manufacturing, and logistics quality, and explain the basis for acceptance decisions.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Quality is not determined solely by the convenience of the manufacturer. The starting point is meeting users’ requirements. Design quality concerns the intended performance and specification; manufacturing quality concerns how these are achieved in actual products; logistics quality concerns delivering the correct items in the correct quantity, on time, and in the required condition. Meeting dimensional requirements alone does not meet the entire requirement if the necessary quantity is not delivered.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: An order requires 80 mounting brackets of the same specification by a specified date. All 80 machined brackets meet the dimensional criteria, but a check after packing finds only 78 in the package. The dimensional result cannot serve as proof that the quantity is correct. Check the packing quantity, label, and shipping record, and consult the responsible person about the shortage.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: QCD stands for quality, cost, and delivery; adding safety gives QCDS. You may not skip inspection to meet a deadline or change material without authorization to reduce cost. Match the requirements, acceptance criteria, and actual results, and confirm any necessary change with an authorized person.

terms.meaning: The quality intended and specified at the design stage.
The performance and condition achieved through manufacturing.
Quality relating to items, quantity, delivery time, and condition until delivery to the customer.
Something that must be satisfied.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-009.summary: Consider quality in relation to requirements. Dimensional acceptance alone does not establish acceptance of quantity or shipping condition.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-010.title: Investigate quality problems through changes in the 4M
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-010.objective: Organize changes in people, equipment, materials, and methods, separating facts from hypotheses about causes.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: The manufacturing 4M are people, machines/equipment, materials/parts, and methods. Checking changes in conditions from these four perspectives helps reduce omissions when quality changes. This is not a classification for assuming that a new operator must be the cause. Check whether a tool change or material-lot change occurred at the same time.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: Hole diameters met the criteria in the morning but the first afternoon measurement was outside them. The records show that both the tool and the operator changed at noon. First identify the last confirmed acceptable result and the first confirmed nonconforming result, then investigate the tool installation, material used, settings, and procedure records. Do not declare one change to be the cause; agree on the investigation sequence with the responsible person.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: The three actuals principle checks facts through the actual place, actual item, and actual conditions. Observe within safe limits and compare the condition with records. After selecting countermeasures, PDCA is needed to compare results with the target and improve. One acceptable item after improvement does not prove that the whole process is stable.

terms.meaning: A way to examine manufacturing conditions through people, machines, materials, and methods.
The actual product or object under consideration.
An explanation or possible cause proposed before verification.
One stage of work within manufacturing.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-010.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Create an imaginary timeline of a dimensional abnormality and, for each of the 4M, make two columns: confirmed facts and matters still to investigate.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not reach into running machinery or remove safety devices to investigate a cause.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-010.summary: The 4M provide investigation perspectives, not proof of a cause. Verify facts and continue monitoring the effectiveness of countermeasures.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.title: Distinguish work standards from QC process charts
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.objective: Distinguish instructions on how to work from quality control items, frequency, and abnormality responses.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: A work standard specifies the work content, sequence, equipment, tools, and important conditions to maintain required quality despite changes in people or time. A QC process chart organizes what is controlled in each process, how often and by what method, and how abnormalities are handled. The working method and the control system play different roles even in the same process.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: In an imaginary cutting process, the work standard specifies how to secure the material and which tool to use. The QC process chart requires checking cut length with a specified instrument at startup and every 30 minutes, segregating affected items and contacting the responsible person if a result is outside the range. Following the working sequence does not permit skipping the 30-minute checks. Conversely, performing the measurement does not justify omitting the securing method.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: When reading a document, verify the applicable item, process, document number, and revision together. If the conditions differ between old and new versions, do not choose one based on experience; ask for confirmation. Before starting, understand how abnormal items are handled, where to record results, and whom to contact. The frequency here is fictional; use the instructions for your actual process.

terms.reading: さぎょうひょうじゅん
terms.meaning: A specification of work content, sequence, methods, and related details.

terms.reading: キューシーこうていず
terms.meaning: A chart summarizing control items, methods, frequency, and abnormality responses for each process.
How often control activities are performed.
Reviewing and changing a document’s content.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: For an imaginary drilling process, make a table separating three items for a work standard from five items for a QC process chart.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not replace approved workplace instructions with the control frequency used in this lesson.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.summary: Work standards specify how to work; QC process charts specify the control system. Check applicability and revision, and follow both.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.title: Choose QC tools to match the purpose
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.objective: Distinguish the uses of check sheets, Pareto charts, histograms, and other QC tools.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Use a check sheet to collect data, a Pareto chart to prioritize categories by counts, and a histogram to examine distributions such as dimensions. A line graph helps show change over time, a control chart monitors process stability, and a scatter plot shows relationships between two quantities. A cause-and-effect diagram organizes possible causes. Decide what you want to judge before creating a chart.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: One week’s appearance defects are recorded as 18 dents, 9 cases of dirt, and 3 cases of discoloration. There are 30 cases in total; Pareto cumulative percentages are 60% through dents, 90% through dirt, and 100% through discoloration. This supports investigating dents first, but a highly dangerous or severe defect must not be postponed simply because its count is low.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: A histogram shows a distribution and does not preserve the original time sequence. A visible relationship in a scatter plot alone does not prove causation. A control chart’s control limits are also different from specification limits used to accept products. Choose the chart and criteria that match the purpose, rather than drawing conclusions from appearance alone.

terms.meaning: A chart using category counts and cumulative percentages to consider priorities.
A chart showing a distribution through frequencies in defined intervals.
A plot showing paired values of two quantities as points.
Boundaries established to monitor process changes on a control chart.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Create four fictional defect categories and counts, then calculate their total and cumulative percentages. Also state which charts you would select for dimensional variation and change over time.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not underestimate a serious safety defect based only on its count.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.summary: Choose a chart according to the investigation purpose. Do not confuse cumulative percentage, causation, and control limits.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.title: Check SI units and prefixes before recording values
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.objective: Distinguish base units from unit conversions and record values with units.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: The seven SI base units are metre m for length, kilogram kg for mass, second s for time, ampere A for electric current, kelvin K for thermodynamic temperature, mole mol for amount of substance, and candela cd for luminous intensity. Workplaces also use mm, g, and ms. Identical numbers with different units represent different quantities, so check the units in the instruction, display, and record field together.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: To record a thickness of 0.8 mm in metres, use 1 mm = 0.001 m, giving 0.0008 m. A mass of 2.4 kg is 2400 g, and a time of 750 ms is 0.75 s. Converting the result back to the original unit helps detect a thousandfold error.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: Uppercase and lowercase letters matter. The unit m indicates length, while the first m in mm is the prefix meaning one thousandth. Mass in kg and force in N are different quantities. Do not rely on the conversational word “weight”; check whether the document asks for mass or force. Keep units in intermediate calculation steps as well.

terms.meaning: A system for expressing quantities in common units.
A quantity describing an object’s amount of matter; its SI base unit is kg.
A symbol placed before a unit to express a multiple or fraction.
Expressing the same quantity in another unit.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Convert 0.35 mm, 1800 g, and 250 ms into m, kg, and s, respectively, and check by reversing each conversion. Also make a table of the seven base-unit correspondences.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Before entering a converted setting into equipment, check the display unit and the approved value.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.summary: Read numbers together with their units. Verify conversions by returning to the original quantity and do not confuse mass with force.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.title: Distinguish inspection scope from nonconforming-item percentage
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.objective: Distinguish incoming, in-process, and shipping inspection, and calculate the percentage with an explicit denominator.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Incoming inspection checks whether purchased items meet specification; in-process inspection checks characteristics during manufacturing; shipping inspection checks whether completed products meet requirements. Full inspection covers every item in scope, while sampling inspection covers specified samples. Do not change sample size, selection method, or acceptance criteria for convenience.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: From a fictional lot of 600 items, 60 are inspected according to the procedure and 3 are nonconforming. The percentage within the sample is 3 ÷ 60 × 100 = 5%. Using 3 ÷ 600 × 100 = 0.5% would incorrectly treat the 540 uninspected items as conforming. The lot’s acceptance must follow the specified acceptance number or other criteria, not the 5% alone.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: One product with two scratches is still one nonconforming item. Do not confuse the count of scratches with the count of nonconforming items. Record whether the result covers all items or only a sample, the period, and the lot number. Sampling informs assessment of the lot’s condition; it does not guarantee that every uninspected item conforms.

terms.meaning: Inspection of delivered purchased items against required specifications.
Inspection of a portion of the population selected by a defined method.
The proportion of nonconforming items in the number of items considered.
A group of products identified and managed under common conditions or similar criteria.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Calculate separately the percentages for 6 nonconforming items among all 240 items and 2 among a sample of 40. State each denominator, population, and whether uninspected items remain, then list further conditions needed for a lot decision.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not mix nonconforming or undecided items with conforming items or send them onward without permission.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.summary: Identify the denominator and population when stating a percentage. A sample percentage alone does not establish the condition of uninspected items or the lot’s acceptance.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.title: Distinguish tensile-test and hardness-test results
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.objective: Distinguish basic stress and strain calculations from the meaning of hardness designations.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: A tensile test applies tensile force to a specimen and examines properties from the force and extension. With original cross-sectional area A and force F, engineering stress is F ÷ A. With original gauge length L and extension ΔL, engineering strain is ΔL ÷ L; multiply by 100 for percent. Testing generally continues to fracture, so the specimen cannot be used unchanged as a product.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
