paragraphs.text: A force of 10000 N on a specimen of cross-sectional area 25 mm² gives engineering stress of 400 N/mm² = 400 MPa. If a gauge length of 50 mm becomes 51 mm while loaded, extension is 1 mm and engineering strain is 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02, or 2%. These values at a single point must not automatically be called ultimate tensile strength or elongation after fracture.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: Hardness testing evaluates another property. Rockwell uses indentation depth, Brinell uses indentation diameter, and Vickers uses diagonal length. HRC, HBW, and HV relate to test methods and conditions, rather than being decorative labels. Do not extract only the number and compare different methods as though they share one scale; assess using the specified method and conditions.

terms.meaning: Force per unit cross-sectional area.
The ratio of length change to the original length.
A reference mark on a specimen for measuring extension.
A component of specified shape pressed into the specimen in a hardness test.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Calculate stress for area 20 mm² and force 6000 N, and strain for gauge length 40 mm and extension 0.8 mm. List the information to check for HRC, HBW, and HV.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Follow the test machine’s entrapment and flying-fragment precautions; do not touch the specimen or fracture area during operation.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.summary: Stress and strain are different quantities. Do not confuse a value at one point with a maximum or a post-fracture value, or treat different hardness scales as identical.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.title: Match nondestructive inspection to the defect’s location
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.objective: Distinguish surface and internal defects and explain conditions for applying inspection methods.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Nondestructive inspection investigates defects without destruction that makes the object unusable. Radiographic testing uses differences in transmission, and ultrasonic testing uses reflections and related signals to investigate the interior. Magnetic particle testing examines the surface or near surface of objects that can be magnetized; penetrant testing examines defects open to the surface. Detectable defects and applicable materials vary by method.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: Suppose visual examination of a weld reveals no obvious crack. This alone does not establish that there is no internal defect. Confirm the required inspection scope and method. Similarly, do not assume magnetic particle testing applies to a nonmagnetic material; ask the inspection specialist to verify compatibility between material and method.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: Sensory inspection uses sight, hearing, and other senses, but should align lighting, reference samples, and acceptance criteria rather than rely only on individual impressions. “No abnormality detected” is a result under specified conditions; no method necessarily detects every defect. Record the method, scope, and conditions together with the result.

terms.meaning: Inspection of defects and related conditions without destroying the object.

terms.reading: しんとうたんしょうしけん
terms.meaning: A test using penetrant to examine defects open to the surface.

terms.reading: じふんたんしょうしけん
terms.meaning: A test using magnetization and magnetic particles to investigate surface or near-surface defects.
Inspection using human senses.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: For an open surface crack, an internal cavity, and uneven appearance color, make a table of inspection methods to discuss and additional material/condition checks.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not enter radiation-controlled areas. Chemical-based and specialist inspections require the applicable qualifications, training, work authorization, and procedures.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.summary: Confirm the method against defect location and material. An acceptable visual result does not guarantee the interior.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.title: Align pre-measurement conditions and reading methods
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.objective: Explain how parallax, temperature, and instrument condition affect a result.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Measurements are affected by the instrument, operator, temperature, setup, and other factors. Read the scale straight on because an oblique view creates parallax. Check calibration relating the indication to a reference, daily inspection records, and validity; a correct zero alone does not guarantee correctness across the full range.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: Two people measure the same shaft and obtain different readings. One reads the instrument from an angle; the other measures the hot shaft immediately after machining. Before taking an average, align the measurement method and temperature conditions and check again. Record both values, times, and object conditions; do not combine measurements from different conditions without qualification.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: A jig is an aid for holding the object or instrument steadily. A V-block can hold cylindrical objects, but improper clamping force or positioning can cause deformation or tilt. Decide the reference, measurement location, and holding method before measuring. Do not adjust an instrument found to be offset without authorization and continue using it.

terms.meaning: A change in scale reading caused by viewing from a different direction.
Checking the relationship between a reference and an instrument’s indication.
A tool that assists work, for example by holding an object or instrument.
The zero position used as the basis of a measurement.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Make a checklist for disagreement between two operators’ measurements, covering viewing direction, temperature, measurement location, instrument, and holding method.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not handle hot machined objects with bare hands; follow cooling and handling procedures.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.summary: Align measurement conditions before comparing values. Zero checks, daily inspection, and calibration are not the same activity.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.title: Use caliper measuring faces and the vernier correctly
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.objective: Select faces for outside, inside, and depth measurements, and add the main and vernier readings.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: Calipers have outside and inside jaws; models with a depth bar also measure depth. Choose the correct measuring faces and check cleanliness, smooth movement, play, gaps when closed, and zero. Clean the workpiece too, and handle burrs using the approved method. Squeezing harder does not necessarily improve accuracy.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: With a 0.05 mm least-reading vernier caliper, a main-scale reading of 18 mm and alignment at the fourth vernier division give 4 × 0.05 = 0.20 mm on the vernier. The total is 18.20 mm. Check the instrument’s least reading first so the fourth division is not interpreted as 0.4 mm. This is a calculation example; actual alignment must be read straight on at the instrument.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: For outside dimensions, hold the part steadily as near the root of the jaws as practicable and avoid reading while tilted. For inside and depth measurements, also check contact with the object. Digital display resolution and measurement accuracy are different. A fine display alone does not establish suitability for judging a required tolerance; use the specified instrument.

terms.meaning: An instrument using a slider and jaws to measure dimensions.
A scale for reading fractions smaller than the main-scale divisions.
Parts that grip the workpiece or contact its inside surfaces.

terms.reading: さいしょうよみとりち
terms.meaning: The smallest increment read from the instrument’s scale.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Calculate a reading with a least reading of 0.05 mm, main scale 12 mm, and the seventh vernier division aligned. Also identify the measuring faces for outside diameter, hole diameter, and groove depth.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not use calipers on rotating stock or parts on moving machinery.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.summary: Check measuring faces and least reading first. Add main and vernier values, and do not confuse display resolution with accuracy.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.title: Check micrometer measuring force and the half-millimetre mark
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.objective: Align temperature and measuring force, then add sleeve and thimble readings.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: An outside micrometer grips the object between the screw-driven spindle and the fixed anvil. Clean the measuring faces and check zero or the datum using a reference suitable for the range. Let the instrument and object acclimatize to the specified environment to reduce temperature effects. The textbook gives 20°C as the reference. Rushing to measure a hot product makes dimensional comparison inappropriate.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: For a 0.5 mm screw pitch and a thimble divided into 50 divisions per revolution, one division is 0.01 mm. If the sleeve shows 7.5 mm and the thimble shows 0.23 mm, the result is 7.73 mm. Reading only 7 mm and missing the half-millimetre mark creates a 0.5 mm error. First identify the last visible sleeve graduation.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: After contact, use the specified constant-force device and do not overtighten. Follow the instrument instructions for how to use it and how many operations are required. Do not select a reading obtained by excessive tightening as the correct one; align posture and contact before reading. Do not add digits without authorization, and follow the procedure for recorded digits and units.

terms.meaning: An instrument using screw motion for precise dimensional measurement.
The measuring shaft moved by the screw mechanism.
The cylindrical portion carrying the reference scale.
A mechanism for applying consistent measuring force.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: For pitch 0.5 mm and 50 divisions, add a sleeve reading of 9.5 mm to a thimble reading of 0.17 mm. Write the sequence for temperature, cleaning, datum, and force checks.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not measure workpieces during operation; follow safe procedures for hot objects and sharp burrs.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.summary: Avoid missing the half-millimetre mark. Align temperature and measuring force and do not overtighten.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.title: Read drawings through scale and line types
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.objective: Distinguish drawing size from actual size and identify outlines, dimension lines, hidden lines, and centre lines.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: A 1:1 scale is full size, 2:1 is an enlargement to twice the actual size, and 1:2 is a reduction to half size. Written dimensions indicate the object’s actual size regardless of scale. Screen magnification or print size may also change, so do not determine machining dimensions solely by measuring the screen or paper with a ruler.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: On a part drawing at 2:1, a feature is dimensioned as 12. The feature may appear about 24 mm long on the drawing, but the specified actual size is 12 mm. In a separate scale-calculation exercise stating “30 mm on the drawing at 1:5,” the actual size is 30 × 5 = 150 mm. Distinguish reading a dimension instruction from a scale-calculation exercise.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: Visible outlines use thick continuous lines; dimension and extension lines use thin continuous lines; hidden outlines use dashed lines; centres normally use thin chain lines with one dash and one dot. Mistaking a centre line for an outline changes the interpreted shape. Part drawings support machining, assembly drawings support assembly, and layout drawings show equipment positions; check the suitable drawing and revision for the task.

terms.meaning: The ratio of size on a drawing to actual size.
A scale that depicts the object larger than its actual size.
A line depicting the shape of a hidden part.
A line indicating the centre of a shape.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: Calculate actual size for 45 mm on a drawing at 1:2. Separately state actual size when a drawing at 2:1 is dimensioned 8, and explain the difference between the two decisions.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not guess indistinct lines or unreadable dimensions and proceed with machining.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.summary: Read specified dimensions as actual sizes. Check scale, display magnification, and line meaning separately.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.title: Read dimensional tolerances and supplementary symbols
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.objective: Calculate upper and lower limits, judge measurements, and distinguish diameter, radius, and thickness symbols.

paragraphs.title: Principle and decision criteria
paragraphs.text: A dimension has a permitted range; the difference between its upper and lower limits is the tolerance. In a display adding signed deviations to a nominal dimension, the upper entry is the upper deviation and the lower entry is the lower deviation. Add them with their signs to obtain limit dimensions. Do not treat the two numbers as unsigned magnitudes and add or subtract by appearance.

paragraphs.title: Organize the workplace example
paragraphs.text: An imaginary shaft has nominal size 20 mm, upper deviation +0.04 mm, and lower deviation −0.02 mm. The upper limit is 20.04 mm, the lower limit 19.98 mm, and the tolerance 0.06 mm. In a simple limit comparison, 20.03 mm is in range and 19.97 mm is outside. However, readings near a limit must follow the specified measuring method and decision rule; do not round for convenience.

paragraphs.title: Records and common mistakes
paragraphs.text: φ denotes diameter, R radius, and t thickness. φ10 and R10 are not the same size; a circle with R10 has diameter 20. Tolerance-class uppercase letters are used for holes and lowercase letters for shafts; consult the appropriate table for numerical ranges. Do not infer the actual fit from the letter’s position alone; check the limit dimensions of both the mating hole and shaft.

terms.meaning: The difference between the maximum and minimum permitted dimensions.
A permitted difference from the nominal dimension.
The length joining two points on a circle through its centre.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its circumference.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.activity:
4 min: Read the terms and identify the judgment in this lesson.
10 min: Read the explanation and separately note conditions and conclusions.
7 min: Rewrite the case decision with its grounds.
7 min: For nominal size 15 mm, upper deviation +0.03 mm, and lower deviation −0.01 mm, calculate both limits and the tolerance, then judge 14.98, 15.00, and 15.03 mm. Explain φ6, R6, and t6 in words.
2 min: Record key points and remaining questions.
safety: Do not accept out-of-limit products through unauthorized alteration or rounding of measurements.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.summary: Calculate limits with the signs included. Distinguish tolerance from deviation and diameter from radius.

mfg1-electrical-l009.title: Build reports, updates, and requests for advice from facts
mfg1-electrical-l009.objective: Distinguish reporting progress, sharing information, and asking about uncertainties; separate facts from assumptions.

paragraphs.title: Make the purpose clear
paragraphs.text:
Reporting communicates work progress or results; sharing information delivers what relevant people need; consultation asks about a decision or response to a problem. One event may require all three. If a part shortage stops work, report the stoppage, inform the next process of its impact, and consult the responsible person about whether substitutes may be used.
State the conclusion first, followed by location, time, item, quantity, and current condition. A long explanation still delays action if the decision you are requesting is unclear. Greeting colleagues and building an approachable relationship also help abnormalities get reported early.

paragraphs.title: Observed facts and possible causes
paragraphs.text:
“The connector is burnt” is more definite than “There is discoloration around the terminal.” If discoloration is all you have observed, report that fact and say that heating as the cause has not been confirmed. Do not report an unchecked quantity as though all items had been inspected.
Sending a message does not guarantee the recipient received its meaning. Repeat back the scope of stoppage, handling of held products, and who checks next, and record instructions. Even in a hurry, consult before making changes outside your authority.

paragraphs.title: Example of a clear report
paragraphs.text: Afternoon assembly requires 40 parts, but the designated box contains only 27 with the correct part number. A report could be: “Part A is short by 13, so this process is stopped. I have confirmed the 27 in the designated box, but other storage locations are unchecked. Please confirm how to replenish them and inform the next process.” Show the basis: 40 required − 27 confirmed = 13 short. Do not claim there is no stock in locations you have not checked.

terms.meaning: Communicating work progress or results.
Delivering necessary information to relevant people.
Seeking advice or instructions about a decision or response.
Repeating received information to confirm understanding.

mfg1-electrical-l009.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, example analysis 7 min, writing 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: With 65 required, 48 confirmed in stock, and other shelves unchecked, write a report in Japanese including the quantity calculation. Separately write what to tell the next process and what to ask the responsible person.
Self-check: Did you show a shortage of 17, avoid stating unchecked information as fact, and specify the decision needed?
safety: If an abnormality affects safety, do not delay evacuation or emergency notification while preparing a detailed explanation.
Do not use substitute parts or lift a stop instruction without authorization.
mfg1-electrical-l009.summary: State the conclusion and facts first. Separate unconfirmed causes from observed conditions and repeat instructions back.

mfg1-electrical-l010.title: From hazard prediction to checking countermeasures
mfg1-electrical-l010.objective: Connect hazard identification, selection of priorities, concrete measures, and checks after implementation.

paragraphs.title: Describe the chain leading to injury
paragraphs.text:
Do not end hazard prediction with “That is dangerous.” Explain what may move, how it may move, who may be affected, and what injury could follow. For a heavy power unit at a bench edge, the chain might be: vibration or contact causes it to fall and strike a nearby person’s foot.
In KYT, people identify hazards, select important points, discuss measures, and decide team actions. Speaking a slogan together is not the goal by itself; create conditions in which the action can actually be carried out.

paragraphs.title: Implementation is not the end
paragraphs.text:
Risk evaluation considers possible harm along with likelihood or frequency of exposure. Use the workplace evaluation method rather than inventing scores or acceptance limits yourself. Give concrete attention to the greater risks first.
A measure needs a responsible person, a deadline, and a check method. “Be careful” alone makes it difficult to verify what changed. Review actual conditions such as storage location, securing method, and access boundaries. After implementation, check that no new hazards were introduced and improve further if necessary.

paragraphs.title: Example: an unstable temporary location
paragraphs.text: A stand holding a small control cabinet is wobbling. First keep people from touching it and report to the responsible person. Decide who will move it and how, using an approved stable location and suitable handling equipment. Afterwards, check stability and the effect on walkways. A promise that “two of us will be careful” does not remove the instability of the stand itself.

terms.meaning: Anticipating hazardous events before work.
Injury or loss resulting from an accident or similar event.
A concrete method to reduce a hazard or problem.
Judging a level or result against criteria.

mfg1-electrical-l010.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, hazard chain 7 min, countermeasure table 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: For a heavy unit at the bench edge, write one chain: hazard source → event → injury. Create a table with the measure, responsible person, deadline, and check method. Add one risk remaining after the measure.
Self-check: Did you describe how physical conditions or layout change, rather than stopping at a warning?
safety: Do not hold falling equipment with bare hands or move a heavy unit alone.
Hazard removal and relocation must use approved methods and assigned personnel.
mfg1-electrical-l010.summary: Explain hazards through cause and consequence. Specify responsibility, deadline, and verification, then review conditions after implementation.

mfg1-electrical-l011.title: Distinguish variation from specifications
mfg1-electrical-l011.objective: Separate the spread of measurements from the allowed range and explain the purposes of histograms and control charts.

paragraphs.title: An average is not enough
paragraphs.text:
Even with the same settings, dimensions vary because of materials, tools, measurement conditions, and other factors. A mean close to target can still include out-of-specification products if the spread is large. Do not conclude that every item passes from the average alone.
A histogram groups values into intervals and counts them to examine the distribution. Check where values concentrate, how widely they spread, and whether any are separated from the rest. Do not infer the entire process distribution from only a few measurements.

paragraphs.title: Specifications and process stability
paragraphs.text:
Upper and lower specification limits define the permitted range required for the product. A control chart instead arranges measurements in time order to examine stability and signs of change. Control limits and specification limits do not have the same purpose or method of determination.
Even while values remain within specification, a continuing shift in one direction may call for investigation. Conversely, an out-of-specification product cannot be shipped just because its value lies within control limits. Judge product acceptance and monitor the process separately.

paragraphs.title: Check with numbers
paragraphs.text: Suppose a training example allows 9.90–10.10 mm. Three measurements are 9.80, 10.00, and 10.20 mm. Their mean is (9.80 + 10.00 + 10.20) ÷ 3 = 10.00 mm, but the two outer values are outside specification. A centered mean does not guarantee individual conformity. These three points also cannot establish adequate process capability.

terms.meaning: Differences and spread among values.
The boundaries of the permitted product range.
A chart using time-ordered data to monitor process conditions.
How many values occur within different ranges.

mfg1-electrical-l011.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, mean example 7 min, written comparison 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: For an allowed range of 19.90–20.10 mm, judge 19.85, 20.00, and 20.15 mm individually and calculate their mean. Then write one sentence each about what you would examine with a histogram and a control chart.
Self-check: Can you explain that two items are outside specification despite a 20.00 mm mean, without equating control limits with specification limits?
safety: Do not hide out-of-specification values by averaging or rounding.
Do not remove abnormal data without authorization; follow workplace procedures for holding products and investigating causes.
mfg1-electrical-l011.summary: The mean, variation, and conformity are different information. Use distribution and time-series charts for their different purposes.

mfg1-electrical-l012.title: Use a Pareto chart to consider improvement priorities
mfg1-electrical-l012.objective: Calculate counts and cumulative percentages, distinguishing frequency from severity.

paragraphs.title: Agree on counting rules first
paragraphs.text:
Before improvement, agree on what counts as one event, the collection period, target process, and categories. If one product has two defects, defect occurrences and defective products give different totals. Without a defined check sheet, collected figures may not be comparable later.
A Pareto chart orders category counts from highest to lowest and shows cumulative percentages. It helps identify categories accounting for many occurrences, but the labels in the chart do not by themselves prove root causes.

paragraphs.title: Counts alone do not determine priority
paragraphs.text:
Sum all counts, then calculate each percentage as category count ÷ total × 100. Add percentages from the largest category to obtain cumulative percentages. Do not directly compare counts collected under different conditions.
Even infrequent defects may require priority if they could cause serious harm such as electric shock or fire. Identify frequent categories with the chart while separately assessing safety and customer impact. Verify improvements using the same definitions and conditions.

paragraphs.title: Independent counting example
paragraphs.text: For the same period and target, each defect is assigned one category: labeling errors 18, scratches 9, missing parts 3. Total: 30. Percentages: 60%, 30%, 10%. Cumulative percentages in descending order: 60%, 90%, 100%. Labeling errors and scratches account for 90%, but missing safety parts cannot be postponed merely because there are fewer of them.

terms.meaning: The number of events counted under a definition.
The proportion obtained by adding categories in order.
Grouping items by a defined criterion.
The magnitude of the consequences if an event occurs.

mfg1-electrical-l012.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, percentage calculation 7 min, tally table 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Order defect counts of 12, 6, and 2 from highest to lowest; calculate total, individual percentages, and cumulative percentages. Explain the difference between defects per product and defective-product count. Write one condition requiring priority beyond frequency.
Self-check: Are the total 20, individual percentages 60/30/10%, and cumulative percentages 60/90/100%?
safety: Do not postpone a serious safety defect merely because it is infrequent.
Do not regroup inconvenient categories to make figures appear smaller.
mfg1-electrical-l012.summary: Unify counting rules before making a Pareto chart. Assess frequency and severity separately.

mfg1-electrical-l013.title: Read drawing scales and line meanings
mfg1-electrical-l013.objective: Distinguish scale from line functions and verify processing requirements using specified dimensions.

paragraphs.title: Drawing size and actual size
paragraphs.text:
Full scale 1:1 draws the object at actual size, enlarged scale 2:1 at twice its size, and reduced scale 1:2 at half its size. Enlarging a drawing does not double the dimension value written on it. Read a dimension value as the actual dimension of the object.
Copying and screen display can alter drawing size. Do not treat a ruler measurement from a screen or printed drawing as the product dimension. Check written dimensions, units, notes, and revision, and clarify uncertainties before processing.

paragraphs.title: Lines express visibility and purpose
paragraphs.text:
Thick continuous lines show visible outlines; thin continuous lines serve purposes such as dimension lines; thin chain lines show centers; dashed lines show hidden features. Similar-looking lines can mean different things depending on thickness and pattern. Do not mistake a hole centerline for a cutting outline.
An enlarged portion alone may not show hidden features or datum surfaces. Compare related views, sections, and notes to determine which surface and endpoint define each dimension before work.

paragraphs.title: Scale calculation and work decisions
paragraphs.text: In a training drawing at 1:5, an actual width of 80 mm is drawn as 80 ÷ 5 = 16 mm. If the paper is reduced again when copied, a ruler may no longer show 16 mm. The dimension annotation of 80 mm remains the basis for the actual width. Do not change material width because the picture appears small.

terms.meaning: The ratio of a drawing length to the actual length.
A scale drawing larger than actual size.
A scale drawing smaller than actual size.
A line indicating a center or axis.

mfg1-electrical-l013.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, scale calculations 7 min, drawing checklist 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Calculate the drawn length of an actual 45 mm at 2:1 and 1:2. Make a table of the uses of outline, dimension, center, and hidden lines. Write a question in Japanese for a mismatch between screen measurement and the dimension annotation.
Self-check: Do you obtain 90 mm and 22.5 mm while explaining that the actual dimension remains 45 mm?
safety: Do not start processing by guessing from a drawing with missing dimensions or an unclear revision.
Do not decide hole or cut positions while line meanings remain uncertain.
mfg1-electrical-l013.summary: Scale changes the representation, not the specified product dimension. Read line types together with dimensional references.

mfg1-electrical-l014.title: Use layout and connection drawings for different purposes
mfg1-electrical-l014.objective: Read physical position separately from electrical connections and match components and terminals across drawings.

paragraphs.title: Choose a drawing for the question
paragraphs.text:
A layout drawing helps check where equipment goes and the space needed for installation or maintenance. A connection drawing helps check which equipment or terminal connects where. Positions on a drawing do not necessarily show the order in which current flows.
A system diagram helps understand the overall electrical system, while circuit or schematic connection drawings help explain operating relationships. Names and conventions may differ by workplace, so check titles, legends, and notes.

paragraphs.title: Trace names and terminal numbers
paragraphs.text:
When drawings span several sheets, match equipment symbols, part numbers, and terminal numbers. Do not connect items simply because they are drawn close together. Similar names do not make different numbers or signals the same connection.
Old standards and industry conventions can coexist. Rather than memorizing only one symbol shape, check the standards and legend applicable to the drawing. Read contact behavior together with equipment state: an a contact closes when operated, while a b contact opens when operated.

paragraphs.title: When drawings disagree
paragraphs.text: Even if layout terminal block TB2 is on the left, a connection instruction to TB1-3 does not permit connection to TB2 merely because it is nearby. Verify revision and equipment identification and hold the connection until the discrepancy is resolved. Physical layout, component identification, and destination must agree.

terms.meaning: A drawing showing component or equipment positions.
A drawing showing electrical connections between equipment or terminals.
A number identifying a terminal to be connected.
The part explaining symbols and conventions used in a drawing.

mfg1-electrical-l014.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, discrepancy example 7 min, matching notes 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Identify which drawing answers “component location,” “terminal connections,” and “overall power system.” List revision, equipment symbols, and terminal-number checks for a TB1-3/TB2-3 discrepancy.
Self-check: Do you resolve disagreement instead of connecting whichever component is closest?
safety: Compare drawings using de-energized teaching materials or approved work conditions; do not change real equipment wiring without authorization.
Do not replace a safety contact with a different type merely because behavior appears similar.
mfg1-electrical-l014.summary: Layout shows positions; connection drawings show electrical relationships. Match equipment identifiers and terminal numbers across drawings.

mfg1-electrical-l015.title: Distinguish conducting, magnetic, and insulating materials
mfg1-electrical-l015.objective: Separate material roles from usage conditions and apply the official correction to insulating-material classification.

paragraphs.title: Do not confuse the three roles
paragraphs.text:
Conducting materials carry current; copper and aluminum are used for wires according to application. Magnetic materials use magnetic effects, as in transformer cores. Insulating materials resist current and separate conductors. Different materials fulfill these roles even within one component.
High conductivity does not make a material optimal for every condition. Also check weight, workability, temperature, mechanical strength, and joining method. Aluminum conducts electricity but cannot be treated as the same magnetic material as iron.

paragraphs.title: A material name alone does not guarantee insulation
paragraphs.text:
Insulating performance can change with overheating, dirt, damage, and aging. Check thermal class, operating temperature, environment, and required thickness against specifications. Do not assume safety just because something looks like plastic or rubber.
This lesson applies the October 1, 2026 errata. Remove “natural rubber” from the inorganic insulating examples on printed page 70 of the uploaded PDF; the inorganic examples are mica and ceramic. Do not memorize natural rubber as an inorganic material.

paragraphs.title: Example: select by role
paragraphs.text: In a transformer teaching model, the current-carrying winding, flux-carrying core, and insulation separating windings have different roles. Use a conducting material for the winding, an appropriate magnetic material for the core, and an appropriate insulating material for separation. Specifications determine actual grades and temperature ratings; this model explanation does not authorize substitute materials in real products.

terms.meaning: A material used to carry electricity.
A material used for magnetic effects.
A material that resists current and separates conductors.
The ability to retain performance under heat.

mfg1-electrical-l015.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, role example 7 min, comparison table 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Tabulate the roles and conditions to check for windings, core, and insulation. Select inorganic insulating examples from natural rubber, mica, and ceramic, and explain why natural rubber is excluded.
Self-check: Do you identify mica and ceramic without assuming suitability from a material name alone?
safety: If insulation is damaged or discolored, do not touch it to test safety; report under the prescribed procedure.
Do not substitute materials or repair insulation without authorization.
mfg1-electrical-l015.summary: Conducting, magnetic, and insulating materials serve different roles. Apply the errata and verify both material and usage conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l016.title: Read resistor markings and tolerance
mfg1-electrical-l016.objective: Calculate a four-band resistor color code and check tolerance separately from ratings.

paragraphs.title: Read the four bands separately
paragraphs.text:
For a common four-band marking, the first two bands are significant digits, the third is a multiplier, and the last is tolerance. The digit colors are black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, and white 9. Gold tolerance is ±5%; silver is ±10%.
Do not apply this method unchanged to components with another band count or special markings. Check the specification if reading direction or band meaning is unclear. Do not infer the original value of a burnt component solely from its remaining colors.

paragraphs.title: Nominal value and range
paragraphs.text:
Tolerance indicates the allowed deviation from a nominal value. For 330 Ω at ±5%, 330 × 0.05 = 16.5 Ω, giving a calculated range of 313.5–346.5 Ω. Actual incoming acceptance follows measurement conditions and component specifications.
Equal resistance does not imply equal power rating, operating temperature, or size. Reading the resistance from a color code does not establish that another resistor is a suitable replacement.

paragraphs.title: Independent reading example
paragraphs.text: Orange–orange–brown–gold gives significant digits 33, multiplier 10¹, and tolerance ±5%. Thus 33 × 10 = 330 Ω, also written as 0.330 kΩ. Joining all color digits to make 331 Ω is incorrect: the third band sets a multiplying factor, not another digit.

terms.meaning: The reference value specified in a component marking.
The permitted deviation from a reference value.
A number by which another value is multiplied.
The power permitted for a component under specified conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l016.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, colors and tolerance 7 min, written calculation 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Read yellow–violet–red–gold as a four-band marking and express the nominal resistance in Ω and kΩ. Calculate the ±5% range and write two specifications besides resistance to check before replacement.
Self-check: Do you obtain 47 × 100 = 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ, a range of 4465–4935 Ω, and separate rating checks?
safety: Do not measure resistance on an energized circuit. Follow procedures for isolation and residual charge.
Do not touch a resistor immediately after heating or replace it solely because the resistance value matches.
mfg1-electrical-l016.summary: Separate significant digits, multiplier, and tolerance. Check resistance and other specifications such as power rating independently.

mfg1-electrical-l017.title: Calculate series and parallel circuits
mfg1-electrical-l017.objective: Find equivalent resistance, voltage, and current in ideal DC resistor circuits.

paragraphs.title: Identify what is common
paragraphs.text:
Two resistors in a single series path carry the same current. Equivalent resistance is R = R1 + R2; voltages are V1 = IR1 and V2 = IR2. Supply voltage equals their sum.
In parallel, both ends connect to the same two points, so each resistor has the same voltage. Branch currents are I1 = V/R1 and I2 = V/R2, and total current is their sum. For two resistors, R = R1R2/(R1 + R2); for positive resistances the result is smaller than the smaller resistor.

paragraphs.title: Series example
paragraphs.text: Calculate a 1 kΩ resistor and a 2 kΩ resistor in series across an ideal 12 V DC source. Equivalent resistance is 3 kΩ = 3000 Ω; current is 12 ÷ 3000 = 0.004 A = 4 mA. The 1 kΩ voltage is 4 V and the 2 kΩ voltage is 8 V; check 4 + 8 = 12 V. The larger resistance takes the larger voltage share.

paragraphs.title: Compare with parallel
paragraphs.text: Connect the same 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in parallel across 12 V: branch currents are 12 mA and 6 mA, total 18 mA. Equivalent resistance is (1000 × 2000)/(1000 + 2000) ≈ 666.7 Ω. The same components give very different total current when connected differently. These are ideal calculations; real connections require checks of supply capacity, component ratings, heating, and protection.

terms.meaning: The resistance representing several resistors as one whole.
Division of voltage across series sections.
Division of current among parallel branches.
A separate path in a circuit.

mfg1-electrical-l017.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, comparative calculation 7 min, new conditions 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: With two identical 1 kΩ resistors across 6 V, find equivalent resistance, total current, and voltage across each resistor for series and parallel arrangements. Show unit conversions and checks.
Self-check: Series: 2 kΩ, 3 mA, 3 V each. Parallel: 500 Ω, 12 mA, 6 V each.
safety: Do not use calculation circuits as instructions for rewiring real equipment.
Change connections without power; even teaching circuits need instructor and rating checks before use.
mfg1-electrical-l017.summary: Series has common current; parallel has common voltage. Connection changes alter total current and heating conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l018.title: Understand diode direction and rectification
mfg1-electrical-l018.objective: Distinguish anode, cathode, and forward direction and explain rectification qualitatively.

paragraphs.title: Two terminals and direction
paragraphs.text:
A diode is a semiconductor component with two terminals: anode A and cathode K. In a basic explanation, the anode-to-cathode direction is forward, while the opposite direction resists current. Do not assume it can be fitted either way just because it has two leads.
Actual components have forward voltage, allowable current, reverse voltage ratings, and other conditions. Do not assume reverse current is absolutely zero under every circumstance; use the part within specifications. Intended functions also vary by type, such as Zener diodes.

paragraphs.title: Rectification and mounting checks
paragraphs.text:
In AC, voltage direction changes repeatedly. Using diode directionality can select current corresponding to one direction, which is the basic idea of rectification. The resulting waveform is not necessarily a constant flat DC output immediately.
For mounting, match A/K on the circuit drawing with part polarity markings and board markings. Check the component documentation for band or mark meaning instead of judging from a similar shape. Hold and clarify a polarity mismatch before energization.

paragraphs.title: Explain the teaching model
paragraphs.text: In an idealized single-diode explanation, passing only one side of AC produces intervals with and without current. Reversing the diode reverses which side passes. This illustrates directionality, not a procedure for direct connection to an AC supply. Real rectifier circuits also require appropriate ratings and other components.

terms.meaning: The direction in which a diode more readily conducts.
The direction opposite to forward.
The action of making current flow in one direction.
The voltage limit a component can withstand under specified conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l018.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, directional explanation 7 min, written matching checks 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Explain A, K, and forward direction in words. List three checks for disagreement between circuit and board polarity marks. Explain what is incomplete about “Rectification always produces flat DC.”
Self-check: Do you distinguish directionality from ratings and consider an output that still pulsates?
safety: Do not connect a component directly to household AC to experiment with polarity.
Check uncertain polarity or ratings with documentation and the responsible person rather than energizing to find out.
mfg1-electrical-l018.summary: Diodes have directionality. Distinguish rectification principles, mounting orientation, and real component ratings.

mfg1-electrical-l019.title: Prepare to protect electronic parts from static electricity
mfg1-electrical-l019.objective: Understand static damage and check the bench, clothing, and component handling before work.

paragraphs.title: Prevent damage you cannot see
paragraphs.text:
Static electricity can change characteristics or damage ICs and other electronic parts. Not feeling a discharge and seeing no external defect do not guarantee absence of damage. Arrange precautions before opening packaging, not just checks after work.
A bench, mat, clothing, floor, or shoes alone do not complete protection. Use the workplace-specified combination and verification method and confirm equipment and accessories are in good condition. Conductive static-control measures must also satisfy protection of people from electric shock.

paragraphs.title: Prepare components and the environment
paragraphs.text:
Check required part and material numbers, quantities, deterioration, and damage before work. Identify and organize parts by type, provide adequate space and lighting, and keep unrelated packaging and waste off the static-controlled surface.
Use specified static-protective packaging for transport and storage. The presence of a bag does not mean every bag performs the same way. Clarify handling uncertainties before opening or transferring components. Do not begin with unanswered questions about the work instructions.

paragraphs.title: Example of inadequate preparation
paragraphs.text: Before assembly, ICs are in an ordinary clear bag and there is no verification record for the specified bench mat. Hold opening and have the responsible person check packaging specifications and workplace records. Do not improvise by attaching metal wire; handle parts only after an approved environment is ready. A clean appearance does not justify skipping the procedure.

terms.meaning: A phenomenon involving accumulated electric charge on objects.
Component damage caused by static discharge or related effects.
A condition in which an object carries charge.
Making an item distinguishable from others.

mfg1-electrical-l019.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, preparation example 7 min, pre-start checklist 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Create a pre-start checklist covering bench, clothing, components, packaging, lighting, and instructions. Explain in Japanese what to check before opening ICs supplied in an ordinary bag.
Self-check: Do you avoid treating an unfelt discharge as proof of safety and check both approved static control and electric-shock protection?
safety: Do not connect your body or bench to power equipment without authorization as a static-control measure.
Select PPE for the actual hazard. Do not universally recommend gloves where they may be caught in rotating parts.
mfg1-electrical-l019.summary: Prepare static control before opening parts. Check the specified environment and safety conditions rather than relying on one accessory.

mfg1-electrical-l020.title: Reason about AND and OR in sequence control
mfg1-electrical-l020.objective: Build binary input/output tables and explain the differences between AND, OR, and NOT.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish sequence from conditions
paragraphs.text:
Sequence control advances stages in a predetermined order or procedure. It may use combinations of relays and other components or a PLC program. Separate when events happen from the conditions that produce an output.
Here, 0 means off and 1 means on in a teaching indicator-lamp example. AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one is 1; NOT reverses an input. OR does not mean “only one or the other”: both inputs being 1 also produces 1.

paragraphs.title: Check all four combinations
paragraphs.text:
For A/B combinations 00, 01, 10, and 11, AND outputs are 0, 0, 0, 1, while OR outputs are 0, 1, 1, 1. NOT of A alone gives output 1 at A = 0 and 0 at A = 1. Tables help expose confusion with everyday uses of “or.”
In basic examples using a/NO contacts that close when their inputs turn on, series contacts represent AND and parallel contacts represent OR. This explains logic; it is not sufficient by itself to design a real safety circuit. Failure behavior and safety standards need separate consideration.

paragraphs.title: Read the lamp condition
paragraphs.text: “Lamp L turns on when both A and B are on” specifies AND. At A = 1, B = 0 it stays off; at both 1 it turns on. Changing the wording to “at least one of A or B is on” specifies OR, so A = 1, B = 0 also lights it. Different conditions change output even with the same two inputs.

terms.meaning: AND: true only when all required conditions hold.
OR: true when at least one condition holds.
NOT: inversion of 0 and 1.
A signal supplied to the control.

mfg1-electrical-l020.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, operation table 7 min, written conditions 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Make AND and OR output tables for all four A/B combinations. Compare the results for A = 0, B = 1. Finally explain “at least one” versus “both” in Japanese.
Self-check: Is OR also 1 at 11, and have you avoided certifying a safety circuit from logic alone?
safety: Do not modify real interlocks or safety circuits to match teaching logic without authorization.
Use approved teaching equipment and procedures; do not experiment on machinery while someone is in a hazardous area.
mfg1-electrical-l020.summary: AND requires all, OR at least one, and NOT inverts. Logic calculation and safety-circuit adequacy are separate matters.

mfg1-electrical-l021.title: Distinguish preventive from corrective maintenance
mfg1-electrical-l021.objective: Separate scheduled replacement, condition monitoring, and post-failure action, and preserve evidence in maintenance records.

paragraphs.title: When and on what basis to intervene
paragraphs.text:
Preventive maintenance checks and services equipment before failure to reduce failure occurrence. It can include scheduled replacement based on service period or operating hours. Predictive maintenance monitors conditions such as vibration or temperature and uses signs of deterioration to judge service needs.
Corrective maintenance responds after a fault or failure. Selecting an approach requires considering failure impact, safety, downtime losses, monitoring cost, and replacement cost together. A cheap component is not automatically suitable to run until failure.

paragraphs.title: Replacement count alone does not show merit
paragraphs.text:
Early replacement may reduce unexpected stoppages but may also discard usable parts. Condition monitoring can reduce waste but requires defined targets, management thresholds, measurement methods, and systems. Collecting numbers alone does not establish predictive maintenance.
Record equipment identification, date/time, operating conditions, observations or measurements, differences from normal, and whom you informed. For an unusual sound, note when it occurs and the operating state rather than just “sounds odd”; this supports investigation.

paragraphs.title: Compare three approaches
paragraphs.text: In a teaching example, replacing a part every fixed number of hours is planned preventive maintenance; deciding service from increasing continuously monitored vibration is predictive maintenance; repair after a failure stops the unit is corrective maintenance. Different parts of the same machine may use different approaches. Workers report signs and respect the boundary where maintenance personnel make the decision.

terms.meaning: Checks and servicing before failure to reduce failures.
Maintenance based on signs of deterioration found by condition monitoring.
Action taken after a fault or failure occurs.
An indication that a change or problem may occur.

mfg1-electrical-l021.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, compare three methods 7 min, inspection record 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Classify “replace by operating hours,” “decide service from vibration changes,” and “repair after stoppage.” Write a record for unusual noise with equipment number, date/time, operating conditions, observed facts, and recipient of the report.
Self-check: Do you distinguish strengths and requirements without disassembling or restarting equipment on your own from monitored values?
safety: Removing covers, reaching inside, or restarting for inspection or cleaning must follow assigned responsibilities and isolation procedures.
Do not keep abnormal equipment running merely to gather data.
mfg1-electrical-l021.summary: Distinguish advance planning, condition signs, and post-failure response. Record conditions and facts that support maintenance decisions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-009.title: Measure liquid temperature and specific gravity under consistent conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-009.objective:
Explain why liquid temperature and specific gravity are measured.
Distinguish measurement conditions from concentration-conversion conditions.

paragraphs.title: Temperature is one quality-control condition
paragraphs.text:
The temperature of a process liquid affects film formation and appearance. A setpoint display does not guarantee the entire bath is at the same temperature, so measure at the specified location, time and by the specified method. Check instrument condition and compatibility with the liquid; with a liquid-column thermometer, align your eyes according to the required reading method.
Even within one bath, different measurement positions or process timing change the basis for comparison. When reporting “higher than yesterday,” include position, time and operating condition, not just the number. Do not lean over the bath or approach moving workpieces to take a measurement.

paragraphs.title: Read the hydrometer scale correctly
paragraphs.text:
Specific gravity is the ratio of a material’s density to that of a reference material; distinguish it from density and its units. With a liquid hydrometer, check calibration temperature, sample temperature and scale-reading instructions. Follow the instrument and method requirements for reading the upper or lower meniscus.
Contact with the container or attached bubbles can affect flotation and readings. Confirm a stable condition and record the result. Follow workplace rules for sample quantity and instrument cleaning to avoid contaminating one liquid with another.

paragraphs.title: Conditions for converting specific gravity to concentration
paragraphs.text:
Specific gravity does not uniquely determine component concentrations in every liquid. A conversion table or graph is valid only under its specified conditions, including component, liquid composition and temperature. Do not reuse a table intended for another bath.
If a result is outside the control range, check temperature, reading method and table selection, then report it. Do not identify a deficient ingredient and replenish chemicals from the specific-gravity number alone.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Two workers report different specific-gravity readings from the same bath. One measured a warm sample immediately, while the other waited for the temperature specified in the method. First make the conditions consistent before comparing results. Do not treat the difference as a direct change in composition; record sample temperature and the conversion table’s applicability conditions.

terms.meaning: The temperature of a liquid.
The ratio of a density to the density of a reference material.
The column of liquid inside a narrow tube, such as a thermometer.
A table for converting one quantity to another under specified conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-009.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terminology, 10 on explanations and 6 tabulating the two workers’ conditions. Spend 7 explaining checks for “the same conditions,” then 3 creating a sample record.
safety: Prevent splashes and falls when sampling and measuring.
Do not cross safety barriers or touch heaters to obtain a measurement.
mfg1-surface-lesson-009.summary:
Compare liquid temperature and specific gravity under consistent conditions.
Check hydrometer temperature and reading requirements.
Use a concentration-conversion table suitable for the liquid.

mfg1-surface-lesson-010.title: Determine concentration by neutralization titration
mfg1-surface-lesson-010.objective:
Distinguish the roles of the standard solution and sample.
Calculate concentration from reaction ratios and delivered volume.

paragraphs.title: Use a solution of known concentration
paragraphs.text:
Neutralization titration uses a standard solution of known concentration to determine the amount of acid or base in a measured sample. You need sample volume, standard-solution concentration and volume used in the reaction. Recording a colour change alone is insufficient for a concentration calculation.
Distinguish the observed endpoint, indicated by a colour change, from the equivalence point where reacting quantities correspond stoichiometrically. The analytical procedure specifies the indicator and endpoint judgement. Depending on the acid and base, equivalence-point pH is not necessarily 7.

paragraphs.title: Check volume differences and the reaction equation
paragraphs.text:
The delivered volume from a burette is the final reading minus the initial reading. Do not use the final reading alone. Check the meniscus, bubbles and leaks, and read at the specified eye level and position. A volumetric pipette delivers a specified sample volume.
Check reaction-equation coefficients when calculating. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide react 1:1, but another acid may have a different ratio. If converting mL to L, use consistent units on both sides.

paragraphs.title: Record operations along with results
paragraphs.text:
Retain standard concentration, sample volume, initial and final readings, indicator and sample identity so the calculation can be checked later. If you overshoot the endpoint, do not rewrite a favourable value; repeat the measurement according to the analytical procedure.
Titration is a small-scale analytical operation. Its calculation example does not authorize adding chemicals directly to a production bath. Bath replenishment follows a separate control procedure.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Assume that 10.0 mL of hydrochloric-acid sample consumes 12.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide. With a 1:1 ratio, the standard solution supplies 0.100 × 0.0120 = 0.00120 mol. Acid concentration is 0.00120 ÷ 0.0100 = 0.120 mol/L. This is calculation practice, not a specification for an actual analytical method or control value.

terms.meaning: Analysis using the reaction between an acid and a base to determine quantity.
An analytical solution of known concentration.
The point at which an indicator or another signal determines when to stop.
The point where reacting quantities match stoichiometrically.

mfg1-surface-lesson-010.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on explanations and 6 on calculation. In 7 minutes explain delivery and calculation for initial 1.2 mL and final 13.2 mL, then spend 3 checking for missing records.
safety: Never pipette by mouth. Use the specified suction aid and protective equipment.
Do not mix standards or samples in unidentified containers; follow waste-liquid classifications.
mfg1-surface-lesson-010.summary:
Delivered volume is final minus initial reading.
Check equation coefficients and volume units.
Distinguish endpoint from equivalence point and record analytical conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-011.title: Distinguish mass concentration from molarity
mfg1-surface-lesson-011.objective:
Explain the different quantities represented by g/L and mol/L.
Calculate concentration using solution volume.

paragraphs.title: Read what is divided by what
paragraphs.text:
Mass concentration in g/L is solute mass per volume of solution. Molarity in mol/L is amount of substance per volume of solution. Equal numbers with different units mean different things. Read units as well as numbers on records and chemical labels.
The solute is the dissolved component, the solvent is the dissolving liquid and the solution is the resulting uniform liquid. Distinguish the final solution volume in the denominator from the volume of water added. Dissolving something in 1 L of water does not guarantee a final solution volume of 1 L.

paragraphs.title: Use molar mass
paragraphs.text:
Amount of substance equals mass divided by molar mass. Using g/mol for molar mass and g for mass gives mol. Divide that amount by solution volume in L to obtain molarity.
Molar mass can change depending on whether the chemical formula represents an anhydrous material or a hydrate. Actual analysis also requires purity or concentration certification. Match the label and method instead of borrowing a value from a similarly named chemical.

paragraphs.title: Do not interchange concentration types
paragraphs.text:
g/L, mol/L and mass percentage cannot be replaced by the same numerical value without conditions. Conversions require information such as molar mass or liquid density. Concentration based on reaction equivalents also requires confirmation of reaction conditions. This unit covers mass concentration and molarity.
If the procedure and supplier’s analysis report use different units, check the calculation conditions before deciding replenishment quantities. A correct calculation and permission to add material to a bath are separate matters.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: For a practice solute with molar mass 40.0 g/mol, mass 4.00 g and final solution volume 0.500 L, mass concentration is 4.00 ÷ 0.500 = 8.00 g/L. Amount of substance is 4.00 ÷ 40.0 = 0.100 mol, giving molarity 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/L. This is a paper calculation, not a chemical-preparation instruction.

terms.meaning: A component dissolved in a solution.
The liquid that dissolves the solute.
The mass per mole of a substance.
Amount of substance per litre of solution.

mfg1-surface-lesson-011.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms and 10 organizing units. Calculate the example in 6 minutes, compare a 1.00 L final volume in 7, and check units in 3.
safety: Do not mix or add actual chemicals based on the calculation example.
Control heat generation and splashing during preparation through chemical- and process-specific procedures.
mfg1-surface-lesson-011.summary:
g/L is mass-based; mol/L is amount-of-substance-based.
The denominator is solution volume.
Check the chemical formula, molar mass and units.

mfg1-surface-lesson-012.title: Distinguish acidic oxides from basic oxides
mfg1-surface-lesson-012.objective:
Explain oxide classification with the official errata applied.
Do not confuse reaction partners from classification names.

paragraphs.title: Classify by the reaction partner
paragraphs.text:
An oxide is a compound of oxygen and another element. An acidic oxide reacts with a base to form a salt; a basic oxide reacts with an acid to form a salt. Do not reverse the rule by assuming “acidic” means it reacts with an acid.
The corresponding passage in the original textbook was corrected; this unit follows the official errata dated October 1, 2026. Use corrected knowledge rather than copying the original sentence. Confusing phosphorus-oxide names and formulas are not used here.

paragraphs.title: Organize examples by reaction relationships
paragraphs.text:
Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is an acidic oxide; calcium oxide, CaO, is a basic oxide. On paper, match acidic oxides with the base side and basic oxides with the acid side. Reaction conditions and products are not identical in every case.
Aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, and zinc oxide, ZnO, are amphoteric oxides that can react with both acids and bases. This helps explain relationships between surface oxides and treatment liquids, but does not authorize learners to select process chemicals independently.

paragraphs.title: Keep classification separate from safety
paragraphs.text:
A neutral-oxide classification does not mean safe. Carbon monoxide, CO, is an example of a neutral oxide but is a harmful gas. Do not use “neutral” to mean harmless.
Powders, gases and heated solids require different handling even among oxides. Do not classify an unknown material by experimenting with acids or bases; check its name, formula, SDS and approved procedure.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Sort cards marked CO₂, CaO and Al₂O₃ into reactions with bases, with acids and with both respectively. CO₂ is acidic, CaO basic and Al₂O₃ amphoteric. This is a knowledge exercise, not chemical mixing.

terms.meaning: A compound of oxygen and another element.
An oxide that can react with bases to form salts.

terms.reading: えんきせいさんかぶつ
terms.meaning: An oxide that can react with acids to form salts.

terms.reading: りょうせいさんかぶつ
terms.meaning: An oxide that can react with both acids and bases.

mfg1-surface-lesson-012.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on the correction and classification, and 6 on cards. In 7 minutes explain the error in “neutral means safe,” then summarize in 3.
safety: Do not add unidentified oxides to chemicals to test their reaction.
Do not dismiss carbon-monoxide toxicity because it is classified as neutral.
mfg1-surface-lesson-012.summary:
Acidic oxides react with bases; basic oxides react with acids.
Amphoteric oxides react with both.
Classification names do not guarantee safety.

mfg1-surface-lesson-013.title: Distinguish dissolution and precipitation in a process
mfg1-surface-lesson-013.objective:
Explain solvent, solute and solution.
Relate observations of clear liquids and precipitates to component control.

paragraphs.title: Dissolving means becoming uniformly distributed
paragraphs.text:
A solution is formed when a solute dissolves uniformly in a solvent. In salt water, salt is the solute and water the solvent. Components that are no longer visible have not disappeared; a clear liquid can still contain them.
A solid remaining at the bottom may be incompletely dissolved, exceed solubility, or be a different contaminant. Do not identify composition or quantity from appearance alone; check liquid identity, temperature and mixing history.

paragraphs.title: A reaction can form a sparingly soluble solid
paragraphs.text:
Precipitation occurs when components react and a poorly soluble solid appears. With chloride ions Cl⁻ and silver ions Ag⁺, the relationship Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl represents formation of solid silver chloride. Both charge and atom counts balance.
A white solid is not necessarily silver chloride. Other reactions can produce similar-looking solids. Use an appropriate analytical method and procedure; do not identify a compound from observation alone.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish analysis from a production-bath abnormality
paragraphs.text:
Some analytical methods deliberately form and separate a precipitate to determine quantity. Unexpected precipitation in a production bath instead requires investigation of conditions or contamination. A useful analytical phenomenon is not automatically acceptable in production.
Less precipitate or clearer liquid does not prove all components are correct. Filter or add chemicals only within an approved process, and manage both solids and liquids by prescribed methods.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: White turbidity is found in a bath with a recorded liquid-mixing event. The worker does not independently transfer only the clear portion to the next bath. Report the liquids mixed, time, temperature and turbidity. Do not identify “silver chloride” by colour alone; responsible staff decide analysis and action.

terms.meaning: A substance dissolving uniformly in a solvent.
A uniform liquid containing solute dissolved in solvent.
Formation of a poorly soluble solid through reaction or a related change.
Analysis to determine the quantity of a component.

mfg1-surface-lesson-013.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on explanation and 6 organizing the example report. Explain clear liquid versus components in 7 minutes, then check reaction charges in 3.
safety: Do not directly touch white solids or clear supernatant.
Do not mix process liquids to try out the teaching reaction.
mfg1-surface-lesson-013.summary:
Dissolved components remain even in clear liquids.
Appearance alone cannot identify a precipitate.
Distinguish an analytical purpose from a production-bath abnormality.

mfg1-surface-lesson-014.title: Estimate material mass from density
mfg1-surface-lesson-014.objective:
Calculate the relationship between density, volume and mass.
Distinguish density calculation from material identification.

paragraphs.title: Equal size does not mean equal mass
paragraphs.text:
Density is mass per unit volume, expressed in units such as g/cm³. At equal volume, denser material has more mass. Distinguish density and its units from specific gravity, a ratio to a reference.
The basic calculation is mass = density × volume. For a hollow item or one with holes, subtract void volume from external volume. Do not assume external dimensions describe a completely solid rectangular block.

paragraphs.title: Convert length units first
paragraphs.text:
Converting mm to cm divides length by ten, but volume is affected in three dimensions: 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³. Align units before multiplying; do not directly multiply g/cm³ by mm³.
Representative values serve practice or estimation, while actual density can vary with alloy composition and temperature. Where material certification or drawings specify a value, check its applicability conditions.

paragraphs.title: An estimate does not replace identification or lifting authorization
paragraphs.text:
If calculated and measured mass differ substantially, recheck units, holes, shape, quantity and material. Similar mass alone does not prove identical material or quality.
Do not use an estimate alone to lift a heavy item by yourself or judge lifting-gear capacity. Actual weight, centre of gravity, handling procedure and confirmation by responsible personnel are necessary.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Assume a solid practice aluminium plate of 100 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm and density 2.70 g/cm³. Its volume is 10 cm × 4 cm × 0.5 cm = 20 cm³, so mass is 2.70 × 20 = 54.0 g. Account for cutouts or holes in a real item. This calculation does not identify the material or authorize lifting.

terms.meaning: Mass per unit volume.
The amount of space an object occupies.
A fundamental quantity describing the mass of matter.
Having an internal empty space.

mfg1-surface-lesson-014.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on unit conversion and 6 on the example. In 7 explain the result if plate volume halves; in 3 review identification versus estimation.
safety: Do not choose a lifting method or lifting gear from an estimated mass alone.
Avoid sharp plate edges and swarf; use the prescribed handling method.
mfg1-surface-lesson-014.summary:
Mass = density × volume.
1 cm³ = 1000 mm³.
Estimation is separate from material certification and handling-safety checks.

mfg1-surface-lesson-015.title: Verify the identity of copper, aluminium and zinc alloys
mfg1-surface-lesson-015.objective:
Explain typical copper-alloy combinations.
Check processing from material information rather than appearance.

paragraphs.title: The main component does not fully define an alloy
paragraphs.text:
An alloy combines a principal metal with other elements to adjust properties. Typical copper-based examples are brass with zinc, bronze with tin, and cupronickel with nickel. Actual alloys may have other additions, so a name alone does not reveal exact proportions.
Materials are selected according to priorities such as conductivity, strength and corrosion resistance. Different substrates affect pretreatment and finish; similar-looking items cannot automatically be processed together.

paragraphs.title: Check aluminium and zinc varieties too
paragraphs.text:
Aluminium alloys retain lightness while adjusting properties and are used in machining, forming or casting. A material designation such as ADC12 gives more specific identification than simply saying “aluminium.”
Zinc is used for coatings on ferrous materials and in die-casting alloys. A zinc-alloy substrate and a zinc surface film have different roles. Recording substrate, undercoat and outermost layer separately helps prevent mix-ups.

paragraphs.title: Do not identify unknown material by trial
paragraphs.text:
At receipt, compare drawings, material codes, lot labels and certificates. Do not identify unlabelled material solely by colour or weight, or by testing a reaction in acid. Identify unverified items and route them through an approved verification method.
When materials change, responsible staff check whether existing pretreatment remains suitable and whether required appearance or inspection methods are affected. Verifying material and having authority to change process settings are separate matters.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Two copper-coloured component types arrive in one box; one delivery document says brass and the other bronze. Do not group them by appearance. Separate part numbers and lots, then check material codes and work instructions. Zinc is a typical brass addition and tin a typical bronze addition, but that knowledge alone does not identify individual items.

terms.meaning: A material principally combining a metal with other elements.
An alloy based on copper and zinc.
A typical alloy based on copper and tin.
An alloy based on copper and nickel.

mfg1-surface-lesson-015.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 comparing materials and 6 on the mixed-box example. Explain substrate, undercoat and outermost layer in 7 minutes, then review unidentified-material handling in 3.
safety: Do not place unknown materials in chemicals to identify them.
Obtain approved process-compatibility verification when the material changes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-015.summary:
Distinguish typical alloy combinations from certification of an actual item.
Do not confuse substrate and coating.
Identify, segregate and verify unknown material before processing.

mfg1-surface-lesson-016.title: Control degreasing and activation in sequence
mfg1-surface-lesson-016.objective:
Distinguish oil removal from oxide-film removal.
Check interstage rinsing and processing history.

paragraphs.title: Cleaning stages have different roles
paragraphs.text:
Before electroplating, degreasing removes oils and contamination, while activation removes oxides and prepares the surface. Calling both simply “washing” obscures the defect each stage prevents. Select liquids and methods for the substrate.
Control degreasing concentration, temperature and time. Residual contamination can repel liquid or impair adhesion, but absence of visible oil alone does not prove adequate degreasing. Use the specified verification method.

paragraphs.title: Maintain the activated surface condition
paragraphs.text:
Activation uses chemicals and conditions suited to the substrate surface. Both insufficient and excessive treatment can cause problems; check concentration, temperature, duration and delay before the next stage. A stronger bath or longer immersion is not necessarily better and can be dangerous.
Rinsing after treatment removes the previous liquid and limits carryover to the next bath. Check rinse routing and cleanliness, and do not skip stages. Rinse water is also controlled waste and cannot automatically be discharged untreated.

paragraphs.title: Pass preceding-stage information forward
paragraphs.text:
Record part number, lot, bath, time and conditions so later adhesion defects can be investigated. Identify and report affected items if waiting unexpectedly increases, the wrong bath is used or conditions go out of range.
Returning an item to a previous stage without authorization loses traceability and risks overprocessing or mixing liquids. Responsible staff decide whether and how to reprocess according to material and quality requirements.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: A lot has finished activation but waits longer than planned because equipment stops. Do not decide “another acid dip will fix it.” Record stop time, holding condition, lot and completed stages. The responsible person checks surface condition and procedure before deciding the next action.

terms.meaning: Treatment that removes oil from the surface.
Preparing a surface to be suitable for the next reaction.
Washing off treatment chemicals with water.
Transfer of liquid or other material from one stage into the next.

mfg1-surface-lesson-016.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on stage purposes and 6 on the delay example. Create a processing-history form in 7 minutes, then explain unauthorized reprocessing risks in 3.
safety: Do not independently add chemicals or move items to a different bath.
Check splash/contact hazards and the condition of specified protective equipment and exhaust ventilation.
mfg1-surface-lesson-016.summary:
Degreasing and activation have different purposes.
Rinsing and waiting time are process conditions too.
Record abnormalities and do not independently decide reprocessing.

mfg1-surface-lesson-017.title: Investigate blistering and discolouration through process history
mfg1-surface-lesson-017.objective:
Distinguish blistering, discolouration and unplated areas.
Separate appearance-based hypotheses from confirmed causes.

paragraphs.title: Describe the observed condition precisely
paragraphs.text:
Blistering is a raised film separating from the substrate. Discolouration is a colour change; an unplated area is one that should have received coating but did not. First record location, extent and shape on the item.
“Bad plating” is insufficient information for investigation. Standardize inspection conditions, retain photographs or location sketches, and link discovery time to the lot. Do not polish away the appearance or flatten the blister to conceal it.

paragraphs.title: Trace possible contributing stages
paragraphs.text:
Inadequate pretreatment, such as degreasing or activation, can contribute to blistering or unplated areas. Rinsing, storage, substrate and deposits can contribute to discolouration. Appearance alone does not confirm one cause.
