mfg1-electrical-l032.objective: Distinguish generating from light, storing electricity, and converting DC to AC.

paragraphs.title: Generation and storage are different
paragraphs.text:
A solar cell converts light energy into electricity. Insufficient light reduces generation, and without light at night it cannot generate as during daytime. Although called a “cell,” it differs from a storage battery that stores generated energy for later nighttime use.
Adding storage can save generated energy for later within system conditions. Capacity, charging/discharging, remaining charge, and available functions have limits. Solar panels alone do not guarantee every appliance will always work during an outage.

paragraphs.title: The device linking DC and AC
paragraphs.text:
Solar-cell output is DC. In a system serving ordinary AC equipment, a power conditioner performs functions such as DC-to-AC conversion, adjustment for generation conditions, and abnormality detection.
Do not confuse generation, storage, and conversion as one box’s function. Actual connections require compatibility, protection, grid-related, and outage-behavior checks. This lesson explains system roles, not installation or grid-connection procedures.

paragraphs.title: Check an explanation
paragraphs.text: “It generated during the day, so the solar cell alone delivers the same power at night” is incomplete; nighttime use needs another storage or supply arrangement. “It works in an outage” also requires checking system functions and conditions. No generation does not mean no voltage in equipment or storage batteries.

terms.meaning: A semiconductor device converting light to electricity.
A device charged to store electrical energy for later release.
Current or voltage treated fundamentally as unidirectional.
Changing one form or state into another.

mfg1-electrical-l032.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, role example 7 min, system explanation 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Match “light → generation,” “store electricity,” and “DC → AC” to solar cells, storage batteries, and a power conditioner. Write two conditions to check each for nighttime and outage use.
Self-check: Do you avoid equating low generation with no voltage or guaranteeing outage use unconditionally?
safety: Do not touch solar or battery terminals or wiring without authorization; nighttime or an outage alone does not establish safety.
Do not change real DC/AC wiring or grid connections as an exercise for this lesson.
mfg1-electrical-l032.summary: Solar cells generate, batteries store, and power conditioners convert and perform other functions. Operating conditions and absence-of-voltage checks are separate.

mfg1-electrical-l033.title: Distinguish pressure, flow, and direction in hydraulics
mfg1-electrical-l033.objective: Organize pump, actuator, and valve functions and explain differences in force, speed, and direction.

paragraphs.title: From oil to motion
paragraphs.text:
Hydraulics uses oil flow and pressure to move machinery. Components include a pump, actuators converting hydraulic energy to force or motion, and valves controlling flow. Do not simplify a pump as independently creating constant pressure at any load; consider the circuit and load conditions.
A cylinder gives linear motion, while a hydraulic motor gives rotary motion. Trace where oil flows and which device moves, rather than only recognizing lines in a diagram.

paragraphs.title: Do not confuse three controls
paragraphs.text:
Pressure-control valves adjust pressure, related to actuator force. Flow-control valves adjust flow, related to speed. Directional valves change the flow path and motion direction. Slow movement does not necessarily call for higher pressure.
Actual force and speed also depend on load and circuit conditions. Do not assume turning one adjustment screw solves everything. Report commanded values, pressure/flow state, and the specific motion difference within your assigned role.

paragraphs.title: Classify symptoms
paragraphs.text: “Moves the wrong way,” “correct direction but slow,” and “insufficient force” are different observations in a teaching cylinder. Record them separately as direction, speed, and force information. Classification alone does not prove a particular valve failed. Confirm causes through approved checks before changing settings or disassembling.

terms.meaning: A system transmitting force or motion using oil pressure.
The volume of liquid flowing per unit time.
A valve controlling pressure, flow, direction, or another condition.
A quantity expressing force per area.

mfg1-electrical-l033.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, symptom classification 7 min, function table 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Match pressure-, flow-, and directional-control valves primarily to force, speed, and direction. Write Japanese reports for reverse movement, slowness, and low force, separating observed facts from fault causes.
Self-check: Do you avoid diagnosing a valve from symptoms alone or proposing unauthorized adjustment?
safety: Do not search for oil leaks with a hand or loosen pressurized piping. Follow assigned procedures for residual pressure even after stopping.
Keep out of hazardous areas and verify approved isolation and support against unexpected cylinder or load motion.
mfg1-electrical-l033.summary: Pressure, flow, and direction are different controlled quantities. Separate force, speed, and direction symptoms and verify causes through checks.

mfg1-electrical-l034.title: Protect logistics quality with industrial packaging
mfg1-electrical-l034.objective: Connect storage/transit protection with control of item, quantity, destination, and delivery date.

paragraphs.title: Being in a box is not enough
paragraphs.text:
Industrial packaging preserves product quality during storage and transport. Choose materials suited to shape, weight, fragility, humidity, temperature, and transport method. A large strong outer box can still allow damage if the product moves inside or load presses on terminals.
Clarify each material’s purpose, such as cushioning for shock and fixing material for movement. Electronic products may also need moisture and static protection. Reducing material use still requires meeting protection requirements.

paragraphs.title: Logistics quality is more than avoiding damage
paragraphs.text:
Alongside product quality, meet the promised date and ensure correct item, quantity, and destination. Match product numbers, quantities, and identifiers on packaging and documents. Correct contents sent to the wrong destination do not meet logistics quality.
Handling, keep-dry, and do-not-stack marks tell handlers how to treat cargo. A label alone does not protect it; confirm actual storage and handling follow it. Do not guess the meaning or applicability of a mark.

paragraphs.title: Pre-shipment example
paragraphs.text: A planned box holds six control parts. The quantity is six, but the label shows another part number. Do not ship based on quantity alone; match identification, packaging specification, documents, and destination and request correction. For a do-not-stack box, also check storage and stacking arrangements follow the instruction. A neat-looking box does not justify skipping checks.

terms.meaning: Packaging protecting industrial products during storage and transport.
Material used to soften shock or impact.
Storage, transport, and delivery managed according to requirements.
An instruction not to stack other cargo on the marked package.

mfg1-electrical-l034.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, shipping example 7 min, checklist 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Make checks for internal fixing, shock, moisture, identification, quantity, destination, and date. Write a Japanese report for a contents/label part-number mismatch. Explain why attaching a handling label alone is insufficient.
Self-check: Do you check protection and delivery rather than shipping from quantity agreement alone?
safety: Use specified handling methods for heavy or wooden boxes; watch for collapse, nails, and sharp edges.
Do not stack against instructions or ship products with unclear packaging without authorization.
mfg1-electrical-l034.summary: Match packaging to product and transport conditions. Check item, quantity, destination, and date as well as damage prevention.

mfg1-electrical-l035.title: Injection molding and fiber-reinforced plastics basics
mfg1-electrical-l035.objective: Explain resin types and injection-molding flow and check property differences from materials, conditions, and fibers.

paragraphs.title: How heat changes the material
paragraphs.text:
Thermoplastics use softening with heat and hardening on cooling. A cured thermoset cannot simply be remelted and reshaped in the same way. Check material name, lot, drying, and other conditions; do not mix different resins without authorization.
Injection molding heats resin, fills a mold, then applies holding pressure and cooling as specified before opening and removing the product. Injection unit, clamping unit, and mold serve different functions. Hazards include strong clamping force as well as hot resin.

paragraphs.title: Conditions determining shape and quality
paragraphs.text:
Resin flows through sprue, runner, and gate into the product cavity. Temperature, pressure, amount, speed, cooling, and foreign matter affect the result. When a molding defect appears, record time, location, quantity, and conditions rather than changing one setting without permission.
FRP combines resin with fibers such as glass or carbon. Properties depend on fiber type, orientation, content, and resin. Do not generalize that every FRP is stronger than metal or electrically insulating; check application-specific specifications.

paragraphs.title: Prevent material mix-ups
paragraphs.text: Glass-fiber board material and carbon-fiber components need not have the same electrical properties. Do not substitute based merely on a black appearance or fiber content. Even if molding produces the same shape, appearance may not reveal a wrong material; match identification and loading records.

terms.meaning: A resin that softens with heating and hardens with cooling.

terms.reading: ねつこうかせいじゅし
terms.meaning: A resin that cannot be remelted in the same way after curing.
Forming a product by filling a mold with heated resin.

terms.reading: きょうかぷらすちっく
terms.meaning: A material combining resin with fibers or other reinforcement to improve properties.

mfg1-electrical-l035.activity:
Approximate 30-minute plan: review 3 min, reading 10 min, material comparison 7 min, process organization 7 min, summary 3 min.
Writing: Explain the heat-response difference between thermoplastics and thermosets. Organize injection, clamping, and mold functions and write four conditions to record for a molding defect. Explain in Japanese why FRP is not uniformly an insulating material.
Self-check: Can you explain that equal appearance does not guarantee equal material and that settings are not changed without authorization?
safety: Do not reach between mold halves or disable safety devices. Clearing blockage and mold work require assigned isolation procedures.
Check material information and work procedures for protection and ventilation against hot resin, dust, fibers, and chemicals.
mfg1-electrical-l035.summary: Distinguish resin types and process conditions. FRP properties depend on fibers, resin, and construction; verify specifications.

mfg1-surface-lesson-022.title: Distinguish ammeter and voltmeter connections
mfg1-surface-lesson-022.objective:
Explain why current and voltage are measured.
Distinguish connection principles from authorization to perform the work.

paragraphs.title: First decide what to measure
paragraphs.text:
Current describes electrical flow in a circuit and is expressed in A. Voltage is the potential difference between two points and is expressed in V. Both relate to film formation in plating and anodizing, but they are not the same quantity. Confusing their record fields prevents sound normal/abnormal judgements.
Before measuring, confirm the circuit, AC or DC, expected range and instrument. A displayed number does not prove a valid measurement. Check range, units and instrument condition too.

paragraphs.title: Understand connections through diagrams
paragraphs.text:
In a typical circuit diagram, an ammeter is in series and a voltmeter is in parallel across the two points being measured. Connecting an instrument set for current measurement directly across a power supply can cause a short circuit or other serious hazards. Learning the principle does not authorize rewiring equipment.
For a clamp meter, select a compatible measurement mode and the correct conductor. Check DC/AC suitability and which conductor to enclose; do not assume any number of wires can be clamped together.

paragraphs.title: Report changes with their conditions
paragraphs.text:
When readings differ from before, check comparison conditions such as location, operation, rack loading and contact. One display alone cannot identify instrument failure versus process abnormality. Within your responsibility, record time and observed facts and report them.
Measuring energized parts or changing connections requires specific training, protection and authority. Untrained people must not experiment on operating equipment; use circuit drawings or safe training materials.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: A record says “voltage 12 A.” First verify the measured quantity and unit. 12 A denotes current; do not simply move that number to a voltage field in V. Check the original instrument, measurement time and worker, then follow record-correction procedures.

terms.meaning: An instrument measuring circuit current.
An instrument measuring voltage between two points.
Connection sequentially along one circuit path.
Connection in separate branches between the same two points.

mfg1-surface-lesson-022.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on connections and 6 on the record example. In 7 minutes draw ammeter and voltmeter positions, then review work authorization in 3.
safety: Do not connect an instrument set for current directly in parallel across a supply.
Untrained people must not touch energized parts or change wiring.
mfg1-surface-lesson-022.summary:
Current in A and voltage in V are different quantities.
The basic arrangement is ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.
Use suitable instruments and approved procedures for actual measurements.

mfg1-surface-lesson-023.title: Compare corrosion tests under consistent purposes and conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-023.objective:
Distinguish the purposes of salt-spray and alkali-drop tests.
Do not equate test results directly with service life.

paragraphs.title: Corrosion resistance is tested in different environments
paragraphs.text:
Salt-spray testing examines changes in films and substrates exposed to salt-containing mist. Methods include neutral salt spray, acidic salt spray with acetic acid, and CASS with additional copper chloride. Different methods use different liquids and conditions, so always identify the test.
A longer unchanged period in one test does not mean proportionally longer outdoor life. Tests evaluate prescribed conditions; actual use adds wet/dry cycles, scratches, temperatures and other factors.

paragraphs.title: Specimens and observations are conditions too
paragraphs.text:
Align specimen preparation, positioning, presence of deliberate scratches, observation times and evaluated changes. Confirm whether the criterion is red rust, discolouration, film damage or another phenomenon, and record it. Do not combine distinct phenomena under “rust appeared.”
When comparing lots, check method and specimen conditions as well as duration. Results from different conditions cannot directly establish superiority. Specific settings and pass limits follow the designated standard edition and product requirements.

paragraphs.title: Evaluate resistance to alkali
paragraphs.text:
Alkali-drop testing is used, for example, to evaluate alkali resistance of anodized aluminium films. Apply the specified liquid and judge film changes or time to electrical continuity by the required method. It does not evaluate exactly the same property as salt spray.
Specimens may be exposed to chemicals or heat and no longer remain in their shipment condition. Follow the test operator’s procedure and identify them separately from unused products. Learners must not improvise test-liquid preparation.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Lot A was tested by neutral salt spray and lot B by CASS. Do not conclude B is inferior from time alone; first report that methods differ. Quality staff confirm which results can be compared against the same product requirements.

terms.meaning: Resistance to corrosion.
Applying a salt-containing liquid to specimens as mist.
A sample prepared for testing.
An electrically conducting path becoming connected.

mfg1-surface-lesson-023.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 comparing tests and 6 on the lots. Make a comparison checklist in 7 minutes, then distinguish test time from actual life in 3.
safety: Do not independently prepare, replenish or discard test chemicals.
Watch for residual chemicals or hot specimens and follow the responsible operator’s procedure.
mfg1-surface-lesson-023.summary:
Record test identity, liquid and specimen conditions.
Do not simply compare times from different methods.
Corrosion-test duration is not actual service life itself.

mfg1-surface-lesson-024.title: Check inspection conditions for limit samples and colour matching
mfg1-surface-lesson-024.objective:
Explain how limit samples and colour references are used.
Evaluate under consistent lighting, background and angle.

paragraphs.title: Use a shared visual acceptance basis
paragraphs.text:
Visual inspection uses limit samples illustrating acceptable conditions to reduce individual judgement differences. They are not decorative examples for a vague resemblance check; they establish the defect and allowable boundary. Check part number, revision and storage condition too.
Lighting and viewing direction change how scratches, unevenness and small holes appear. Use the specified source, illuminance, background, distance and angle. Do not invent a favourable condition such as passing a defect because sunlight hid it.

paragraphs.title: Changing light changes perceived colour
paragraphs.text:
Colour matching compares a product with references for target colour or intensity. The same item can look different under daylight, fluorescent light or LED light. Do not compare reference and item under different light.
Fatigue and individual variation matter, so combine visual checks with colorimeter or colour-difference measurements where required. Numerical readings also require appropriate position, optical conditions and reference. Neither human nor instrument inspection is universally sufficient.

paragraphs.title: Appearance does not guarantee other performance
paragraphs.text:
Appearance, adhesion, hardness and solder-wettability tests have different purposes. A colour match does not prove sufficient adhesion. Check each required property using its specified method.
Hold and consult on borderline items instead of changing samples or lighting to obtain a pass. Recording the inspected position and conditions helps investigate differing judgements.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: A part matches the colour reference at the inspection bench but looks redder beside a window. Do not accept or reject it at the window alone. Return it to the specified light source and compare with the reference at the same position and angle. Review instrument colour measurements with quality staff if necessary.

terms.meaning: A reference sample showing an allowable appearance boundary.
A reference showing colour or intensity for comparison.
The illumination reaching a surface.
An instrument evaluating colour differences numerically.

mfg1-surface-lesson-024.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on conditions and 6 on the light-source example. Tabulate purposes of appearance, colour and adhesion checks in 7 minutes, then plan hold records in 3.
safety: Do not independently alter test methods or wipe inspected items with chemicals.
Follow workplace rest or rotation procedures if your eyes become fatigued.
mfg1-surface-lesson-024.summary:
Check sample type and intended use.
Align lighting, background and angle.
Appearance or colour acceptance does not waive other performance tests.

mfg1-surface-lesson-025.title: Use melting point and conductivity for their intended purposes
mfg1-surface-lesson-025.objective:
Explain the difference between melting point and conductivity.
Distinguish representative material values from product conditions.

paragraphs.title: Melting temperature is not allowable service temperature
paragraphs.text:
Melting point is the temperature at which a solid becomes liquid. Representative pure-metal values are about 420°C for zinc and 660°C for aluminium. Alloys may melt over a range; do not apply a pure-metal number directly to an alloy.
Below melting point does not necessarily mean safe service. Strength, dimensional stability, films and bonded joints may be affected well before melting. Use product and material specifications for service temperature.

paragraphs.title: Consider ease of electrical conduction
paragraphs.text:
Conductivity indicates how readily material conducts electricity, in S/m or similar units. Typical pure metals such as silver, copper, gold and aluminium differ, but comparison conditions, temperature and alloy composition change values. Do not determine conductivity from colour.
Even with one material, overall wiring or contact resistance changes with length, cross-section and contact conditions. Highly conductive material does not eliminate poor jig contact or an undersized conductor.

paragraphs.title: Compare several properties
paragraphs.text:
Select materials by combined conductivity, strength, corrosion resistance, weight and machinability. Distinguish aluminium’s low weight from its conductivity differing from copper. Changes require drawing and process approval.
Substrate and film properties also differ. A substrate melting point does not guarantee film heat resistance; an outer metal name alone does not establish electrical-connection performance.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Someone says, “It is aluminium, so it is fine up to 660°C.” This confuses a representative melting point with a service limit. Check the actual alloy, required strength, film and component specification; use approved specifications to judge allowable temperature.

terms.meaning: The temperature where a solid becomes liquid.
A value indicating how readily material conducts electricity.
The area of a cross-section or cut surface.
Electrical resistance arising at a contact.

mfg1-surface-lesson-025.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on both properties and 6 on the temperature example. Organize material-change checks in 7 minutes, then distinguish representative and specified values in 3.
safety: Do not attempt heating or melting from a melting-point table.
Do not substitute conductors or jigs from material names alone.
mfg1-surface-lesson-025.summary:
Melting point differs from allowable service temperature.
Conductivity alone does not determine total connection resistance.
Apply representative values only after checking specifications and conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-026.title: Check compatibility of jigs, masking and tank materials
mfg1-surface-lesson-026.objective:
Distinguish holding, electrical connection and protection.
Check materials against chemical and temperature conditions.

paragraphs.title: A jig does more than hold
paragraphs.text:
Jigs hold or transport items and may also conduct current. Attachment can cause scratches, dents, deformation or jig marks; poor contact may cause insufficient or uneven film. Check orientation and contacts against the standard.
Use and stripping can degrade jigs. Inspect contacts, deformation and coating damage rather than judging only by usage count. Follow material- and process-specific cleaning, stripping and replacement procedures.

paragraphs.title: Protect areas that must not be treated
paragraphs.text:
Masking protects areas where film or chemical action is unwanted. Tapes, coatings and rubbers differ in thermal and chemical resistance. A similar-coloured tape is not necessarily a substitute. Check drawing boundaries and approved materials.
Lifting edges or tears can let liquid enter unintended areas. Do not confuse protected areas with contacts needed for current. Record removal and verification after processing too.

paragraphs.title: Tank materials also have conditions
paragraphs.text:
Tank materials must suit chemical type, concentration, temperature and mechanical conditions. Names such as PVC, PP, FRP or metal do not establish compatibility with every acid or high temperature. Check manufacturer specifications and selection basis.
Report leaks, cracks, discolouration or lifted lining. Independently transferring liquid to another container or repairing with unverified material can cause leaks or chemical mixing.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: The specified tape runs out and someone proposes a visually similar substitute. Compatibility must cover chemicals, temperature, processing time and removal, not just adhesive strength. If approval cannot be confirmed, hold its use and consult the responsible person.

terms.meaning: A tool for holding, transporting and sometimes electrically connecting an item.
Protecting areas that must not be treated.
Material forming a treatment tank.
A protective coating on the inside of a tank or similar equipment.

mfg1-surface-lesson-026.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on the three functions and 6 on substitute tape. Make an inspection list in 7 minutes, then distinguish contact and protected areas in 3.
safety: Do not use unverified tapes, containers or repair materials.
Do not independently strip jigs or repair tanks.
mfg1-surface-lesson-026.summary:
Check jigs for holding and electrical functions.
Follow masking boundaries and material compatibility.
Judge tank suitability by chemical, temperature and other conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-027.title: Distinguish dissociation from metal ionization tendency
mfg1-surface-lesson-027.objective:
Separate electrolyte dissociation from a metal’s tendency to oxidize.
Do not confuse a strong electrolyte with a high concentration.

paragraphs.title: Separate into ions in solution
paragraphs.text:
An electrolyte separates into ions in aqueous solution and carries electrical charge. Positive cations and negative anions are involved. Not every dissolved substance dissociates to the same extent.
Strong versus weak electrolyte concerns the degree of ion separation under the conditions. It does not mean concentrated versus dilute. Read concentration and dissociation extent as separate properties.

paragraphs.title: A metal’s tendency to release electrons
paragraphs.text:
Ionization tendency is a guide to a metal releasing electrons and becoming ions. Zinc and iron, for example, differ. Do not treat electrolyte dissociation degree and metal ionization tendency as the same quantity.
Actual corrosion also depends on environment and films. An oxide film can protect aluminium, so a ranking alone cannot determine an observed corrosion rate.

paragraphs.title: Do not mix materials to test properties
paragraphs.text:
Solution composition, temperature and concentration also affect conductivity. Good conduction does not necessarily mean the target component has the right concentration. Confirm a method appropriate to the analytical purpose.
Metal-chemical reactions can release gas. Do not put metals into acid or energize unidentified liquids to test a ranking. Learn the mechanism through diagrams and records.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: An analysis sheet says “strong electrolyte,” and a worker explains that the liquid must therefore be concentrated. Strength refers to dissociation extent, not the concentration value itself. Verify component, concentration, temperature and method separately, then correct the explanation.

terms.meaning: A substance carrying charge through ions in solution.
The fraction of dissolved components separated into ions.
An ion with positive charge.
A metal’s tendency to release electrons and become ions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-027.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on both concepts and 6 on the report example. Compare concentration, dissociation and ionization tendency in 7 minutes, then review misconceptions in 3.
safety: Do not test by adding metals to acid or energizing unknown liquids.
Manage gas and chemical hazards through dedicated procedures.
mfg1-surface-lesson-027.summary:
Electrolyte strength is not concentration itself.
Dissociation degree and metal ionization tendency differ.
Judge corrosion with films and environment as well.

mfg1-surface-lesson-028.title: Consider deposited mass through charge and current efficiency
mfg1-surface-lesson-028.objective:
Calculate charge from current and time.
Distinguish theoretical from actual deposited mass.

paragraphs.title: Consider duration as well as current
paragraphs.text:
For constant current, charge Q equals current I multiplied by time t. Using A and seconds gives charge in C, coulombs. Equal current with different duration gives different charge. Do not mix minutes and seconds.
A varying-current process cannot simply apply one constant value over its whole duration. Use a treatment consistent with actual records, such as time segments. Distinguish settings from measured records.

paragraphs.title: Not all current produces the intended deposit
paragraphs.text:
Faraday’s law relates electrode-reacted substance quantity to charge. Actual baths have side reactions, such as hydrogen generation; not all supplied current necessarily deposits the desired metal.
Current efficiency represents the share used for the intended deposit. When estimating actual mass by multiplying theoretical mass by efficiency, use 0.80 for 80%. Efficiency depends on bath and conditions, so do not use the example as a fixed production value.

paragraphs.title: Longer time does not necessarily improve quality
paragraphs.text:
Estimated total deposit mass is separate from acceptable thickness uniformity, appearance and adhesion. More total material after longer processing does not necessarily remove local unevenness or defects.
If deposit is below expectation, check current, time, area, contact, bath conditions and measurement method and report it. Do not independently compensate by increasing current or duration.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: For practice, constant 2.0 A for 3 minutes means 3 × 60 = 180 seconds, so Q = 2.0 × 180 = 360 C. In a separate practice condition, theoretical mass 1.00 g at 80% efficiency gives 1.00 × 0.80 = 0.80 g. The two examples check calculations; they do not define a constant or operating conditions for the same bath.

terms.meaning: A quantity calculated as current multiplied by time for constant current.
The unit of electric charge, C.
The fraction of current used for the intended reaction.
A value calculated from theory and assumed conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-028.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on charge and efficiency and 6 on both calculations. In 7 minutes separately calculate charge for 2.0 A over 6 minutes and, under a different condition, 80% of theoretical 1.00 g, then distinguish quality acceptance in 3.
safety: Do not independently increase current or time to compensate for low deposit.
Follow approved equipment procedures for gas generation and power handling.
mfg1-surface-lesson-028.summary:
Constant-current charge equals I × t.
Current efficiency is the share used for the intended reaction.
Estimated mass alone does not guarantee film quality.

mfg1-surface-lesson-029.title: Organize conversion-coating types and their underlayer roles
mfg1-surface-lesson-029.objective:
Distinguish phosphating, chromate, zincate and blackening.
Do not decide chemical species or conditions from names alone.

paragraphs.title: Form a film by reaction at the surface
paragraphs.text:
Conversion treatment uses chemical reaction at a metal surface to create a film with properties different from the substrate. Roles include corrosion protection, paint adhesion and lubricity. Calling every process metal plating confuses purpose and sequence.
Phosphating forms a phosphate-based film and is used, for example, as a paint pretreatment on steel. Check bath/substrate combinations; similar product names do not authorize substitution between chemical systems.

paragraphs.title: Chromium treatments and other pretreatments
paragraphs.text:
Chromate-related processes differ in chromium species and process system. Do not assume hexavalent and trivalent types have identical hazards or performance; check chemicals and product requirements. Nor does every system necessarily have identical self-healing properties.
Zincate forms a zinc film as a pretreatment before plating aluminium alloys and similar materials. Oxide removal and displacement-film formation help later adhesion. Distinguish its role from simply applying a thick main zinc coating.

paragraphs.title: Do not confuse colour with corrosion resistance
paragraphs.text:
Blackening is an example of forming a black oxide film on steel. Dark colour does not establish film thickness or corrosion resistance. Verify quality including required post-treatment and service conditions.
Each chemical has specific hazards and controls. Match environmental and customer substance requirements to current specifications; textbook inclusion does not mean perpetual permission to use it. Do not mix unverified process liquids as substitutes.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: A drawing specifies phosphating before painting, but someone proposes similarly coloured blackening instead. Check required adhesion, corrosion resistance and specified process, not colour. Do not change treatment without approval; discuss the specification differences with responsible staff.

terms.meaning: Treatment forming a film through chemical reaction at the substrate surface.
A general term for salts derived from phosphoric acid.
Pretreatment using a zincate-based treatment system.
Treatment forming a black oxide film on steel or similar material.

mfg1-surface-lesson-029.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on four methods and 6 on substitution. Tabulate purpose, substrate and next stage in 7 minutes, then explain colour versus performance in 3.
safety: Do not independently change or mix chromium-based or other chemicals.
Follow current specifications and dedicated procedures for substance and waste-liquid classifications.
mfg1-surface-lesson-029.summary:
Conversion treatment uses a surface chemical reaction.
Distinguish each method’s purpose and following stage.
Do not substitute or judge performance from colour or name alone.

mfg1-surface-lesson-030.title: Separate coating methods from paint control requirements
mfg1-surface-lesson-030.objective:
Explain relationships among spray, electrodeposition, powder and baking.
Check paint type and curing conditions.

paragraphs.title: Application and curing are different viewpoints
paragraphs.text:
Painting uses a paint film for protection, appearance, slip resistance and other functions. Spraying applies atomized paint; dipping immerses the item. Baking concerns heat curing, so it is not a completely parallel classification to application method.
Electrostatic painting uses electrical attraction; electrodeposition forms a film in a bath using DC. Electrodeposition includes anionic and cationic types. Using electricity does not make every method’s polarity or equipment identical.

paragraphs.title: Powder still requires safety controls
paragraphs.text:
Powder coating applies powdered paint and forms a film through heating or related processes. Even without solvent, dust, ignition, heat and charging hazards require material- and equipment-specific controls. Do not conclude “no solvent means no ventilation.”
Check substrate heat compatibility, pretreatment, thickness and drying/curing conditions. Higher temperature does not necessarily produce a better film faster; consider overheating defects.

paragraphs.title: Match paint labels to the procedure
paragraphs.text:
Water-based versus solvent-based, resin family and one- versus two-component are separate classifications. Two-component products require the specified pairing, ratio and usable time. This lesson does not establish a universal mixing ratio.
Durability depends on formulation, pretreatment, cure and environment, not resin name alone. Avoid claims that water-based means harmless or a resin always lasts longest; check SDS and product specifications.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Only the base of a two-component paint remains, and someone proposes another product’s hardener. Both being “two-component” does not establish compatibility. Match product, specified hardener, ratio and expiry requirements; do not mix if they cannot be confirmed.

terms.meaning: The film formed by paint.
Forming a paint film using electricity in a liquid bath.
Forming a film from applied powder paint.
A film setting and gaining properties through reaction, heating or related processes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-030.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on methods/materials and 6 on the two-component example. Make application, curing and safety checks in 7 minutes, then review name-only judgements in 3.
safety: Do not independently mix different paints, hardeners or solvents.
Follow dust control, ignition prevention and heat-safety procedures even with powder.
mfg1-surface-lesson-030.summary:
Application and curing are different viewpoints.
Match paint classification to use conditions.
Water-based or powder names alone do not establish safety.

mfg1-surface-lesson-031.title: Read plating functions from the application
mfg1-surface-lesson-031.objective:
Distinguish sacrificial protection and barrier effect.
Organize decorative, wear, joining and conductivity purposes.

paragraphs.title: Corrosion protection has several mechanisms
paragraphs.text:
Zinc-based films can protect ferrous substrates by corroding first: sacrificial protection. Nickel or chromium films can act as barriers to oxygen and water. Evaluate actual performance for the material combination and environment.
A film does not permit ignoring scratches or pinholes. Different protective mechanisms mean different effects of defects. A coating name alone does not guarantee the same protection on every substrate.

paragraphs.title: Separate appearance from function
paragraphs.text:
Decorative chromium emphasizes appearance, while hard chromium targets properties such as wear resistance. The same chromium name does not imply equal specifications, thickness or inspection. Similar appearance does not authorize substitution.
Gold and silver plating have decorative and electrical-contact applications. Tin or nickel/gold can serve electronic parts requiring joining. Confirm each layer’s purpose from drawings and process instructions.

paragraphs.title: Connect layer structure and inspection
paragraphs.text:
Copper provides conductivity in wiring and through-holes; alloy plating can target other properties such as magnetism. Good gloss alone does not prove required electrical or mechanical performance.
Record principal function, undercoat/outermost layer and inspection method together. When applications change, do not substitute a similarly coloured plating without authorization; materials, process and quality staff verify suitability.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Two similar-looking parts differ: one needs decoration, the other solder joining. Check layer structure and joining-property tests rather than colour. Passing decorative requirements does not mean passing solder wettability.

terms.meaning: Protection where a coating or another metal corrodes before the substrate.
Blocking oxygen, water or similar ingress.
Resistance to material loss from friction.
Suitability for joining by soldering or a similar process.

mfg1-surface-lesson-031.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on protection/applications and 6 on the parts. Make a function/coating/test table in 7 minutes, then review substitution conditions in 3.
safety: Do not change coating material or layers based only on application or colour.
Designated personnel perform heating and tests for functional verification.
mfg1-surface-lesson-031.summary:
Protection mechanisms depend on coating and substrate.
Check decorative and functional requirements separately.
Connect layer structure and inspection methods to the application.

mfg1-surface-lesson-032.title: Separate rectifier, agitation and filtration functions
mfg1-surface-lesson-032.objective:
Explain the role of each plating-system component.
Do not judge the whole bath normal from a single display.

paragraphs.title: Check power and workpiece handling
paragraphs.text:
A rectifier converts AC to DC and supplies current required for plating. Match current capacity, control method and waveform to the process. Correct settings do not guarantee current reaches the item as intended if contacts or wiring are faulty.
Holding methods include racks, rotating barrels and continuous reel-to-reel processing. Quantity, shape, contact and transport differ, so do not transfer conditions directly between methods.

paragraphs.title: Reduce temperature and concentration differences
paragraphs.text:
Agitation reduces local concentration or temperature differences and may use air or mechanical methods. Temperature control uses heaters, coolers or heat exchangers. These are different functions requiring separate checks.
A normal temperature indication can coexist with nonuniform conditions away from the sensor if circulation or agitation stops. Check unusual sounds, flow or bubbles as prescribed; do not independently alter flow or method.

paragraphs.title: Filtration has a limited removal scope
paragraphs.text:
Filter circulation separates targeted particles through filter media. It does not remove every dissolved component. A clearer liquid does not automatically have correct composition or concentration.
Opening or replacing filters or pumps involves residual chemicals, pressure and restarting hazards. Do not open covers during operation. Trained personnel follow maintenance procedures covering shutdown, isolation and residual-material handling.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Bath temperature is in range, but the filter unit sounds unusual. Do not assume all is well from temperature alone. Report equipment, sound change, time and flow condition. Do not open the running filter to investigate.

terms.meaning: A power device converting AC to DC for supply.
Moving liquid toward a more uniform condition.
Separating targeted particles through filter media.
Repeated flow along a circuit or route.

mfg1-surface-lesson-032.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on functions and 6 on the noise example. Make power, temperature, agitation and filter checks in 7 minutes, then review limits of normal displays in 3.
safety: Do not open running filters or piping.
Do not independently change power, flow or agitation method.
mfg1-surface-lesson-032.summary:
Power, temperature control, agitation and filtration have separate roles.
One normal display does not prove the whole system normal.
Maintenance must control shutdown and residual hazards.

mfg1-surface-lesson-033.title: Distinguish anodizing post-treatment from performance evaluation
mfg1-surface-lesson-033.objective:
Explain colouring, sealing and drying roles.
Understand why performance tests depend on application.

paragraphs.title: Film formation is followed by other stages
paragraphs.text:
Anodizing may be followed by colouring, sealing and drying as required. Colouring changes appearance through methods such as introducing colour into pores; sealing closes pore openings, limits dye leaching and contributes to corrosion resistance. They are not one identical operation to deepen colour.
Sequence and applicability depend on film and use. Hard coatings involve trade-offs with wear resistance, so do not give every product the same sealing conditions. Confirm the specified process and settings.

paragraphs.title: Check equipment and thermal conditions
paragraphs.text:
Electrolytic and post-treatment baths differ in chemistry and temperature. Control tank materials, jigs, power, agitation and temperature for each stage. Material suitable in another bath may not suit a hot sealing solution.
Heat during drying or use affects film, dye and thermal-expansion differences with the substrate; under some conditions it can cause cracks or performance changes. Do not use a textbook example temperature as a universal limit; follow product specifications and approved conditions.

paragraphs.title: Thickness alone is not a performance evaluation
paragraphs.text:
Depending on use, evaluate corrosion, light, wear and electrical-insulation properties as well as thickness. Colour remaining vivid under light and material resisting friction are different requirements.
Do not interpret representative withstand-voltage values as permission to use the actual item as protective insulation against electric shock. Evaluate specified tests, shape, defects and use conditions. Trained personnel conduct electrical tests.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: Two products have equal thickness: an outdoor coloured part and a machine part exposed to wear. Do not call them equivalent from thickness alone. Confirm required tests, such as light resistance for the former and wear resistance for the latter. Follow each product’s instructions for whether and how to seal.

terms.meaning: Post-treatment closing openings of film pores.
Resistance to light-induced changes such as fading.
Ability to withstand voltage under specified conditions.
A component dissolving out into an external liquid or similar medium.

mfg1-surface-lesson-033.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on post-treatment/tests and 6 on the applications. Make an application/treatment/test table in 7 minutes, then explain limits of thickness-only judgement in 3.
safety: Avoid contact with sealing liquids or hot items and follow equipment-specific protection.
Do not use representative withstand-voltage data as a shock-protection guarantee or perform tests without authorization.
mfg1-surface-lesson-033.summary:
Colouring, sealing and drying have different functions.
Post-treatment depends on application and specifications.
Evaluate properties beyond thickness individually.

mfg1-surface-lesson-034.title: Match buffs and compounds to the process purpose
mfg1-surface-lesson-034.objective:
Distinguish buff stiffness from polishing-compound function.
Keep coarse-stage contamination out of finishing.

paragraphs.title: Buff material and structure change behaviour
paragraphs.text:
Stiff-fibre buffs such as sisal are used for coarse scratches or unevenness. Cloth, rayon, felt, wool and sponge differ in stiffness, shape retention and conformity. Softer does not mean suitable for every stage.
Some nonwoven buffs contain abrasive particles. Even with identical outer shape, material and structure change results. Verify part number, purpose and condition rather than choosing a substitute merely because its dimensions fit.

paragraphs.title: Consider particles and supply form
paragraphs.text:
Solid and liquid compounds differ in delivery, splashing and cleaning controls. Particle material and fineness matter too. Names such as red, white or green bars are clues, but colour alone does not establish every product’s composition or use.
Typical processing moves from coarse scratch removal to fine finishing. Grit and roughness guidelines are not automatically equivalent across product systems. Match product specifications to approved combinations.

paragraphs.title: Prevent carryover between stages
paragraphs.text:
A buff or tool retaining coarse particles can create new scratches during finishing. Separate storage, identification and cleaning of roughing and finishing tools, and identify compounds too. Do not simply return a tool dropped on the floor.
Use specified inspections, replacement or servicing for wear, clogging or unevenness. Do not skip speed compatibility and damage checks. Follow safe procedures for adjustment and installation.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: A soft finishing buff is unavailable and someone proposes a cloth buff used in roughing. Being cloth does not mean free of coarse particles. Check history and cleanliness; do not transfer it to finishing without approved preparation.

terms.meaning: A buff material made with stiff natural fibre.
Material formed by bonding fibres without weaving.
Particles that remove material from a surface.
Accumulated particles or dirt impairing a tool’s action.

mfg1-surface-lesson-034.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 on materials/compounds and 6 on reuse. Make roughing/finishing identification and storage rules in 7 minutes, then review colour- or softness-only selection in 3.
safety: Do not install a buff unsuitable for the rotational conditions.
Do not replace or clean rotating tools or improvise compound feeding.
mfg1-surface-lesson-034.summary:
Select buff and compound as separate factors.
Check product, purpose and use history.
Keep coarse particles out of finishing.

mfg1-surface-lesson-035.title: Match polishing machines and holding methods to the work
mfg1-surface-lesson-035.objective:
Explain bench, pedestal, handheld and robotic equipment.
Consider remaining hazards and quality checks despite automation.

paragraphs.title: Machine form changes handling
paragraphs.text:
Bench or pedestal machines bring the item to a fixed rotating tool. Handheld machines move a powered tool to the item and may use electricity or compressed air. Both require controls for rotating-part contact, ejected items and posture.
Small parts, large items and complex surfaces differ in holding and tool access. Being hand-sized does not mean no fixture is needed. Use specified jigs, support and posture; responsible staff select machinery for material and shape.

paragraphs.title: Roles of belts and robots
paragraphs.text:
Belt grinding uses a continuous abrasive belt, for example to prepare flats and corners. It is not the same tool as a soft rotating buff; check cutting action and contact hazards separately.
Robots repeat movements and help stabilize posture and conditions. Unsuitable programming, positioning, holding or tool wear still changes quality. Automatic operation does not waive inspection.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish stopped machinery, entry and quality checks
paragraphs.text:
A robot appearing stopped can restart or retain stored energy. Do not enter its enclosure without authorization or defeat interlocks. Trained personnel perform setup, tool changes and maintenance in an approved safe condition.
Changing machines changes contact and feed even for the same appearance target. Perform trials, first-piece checks and specified inspections; production quantity alone does not establish stability. Record quality results and tool history.

paragraphs.title: Workplace reasoning
paragraphs.text: After scratches appear on robot-polished parts, a worker approaches the buff inside a stopped cell. A stop indication does not authorize entry. Check prescribed stopping, isolation and entry procedures. Responsible personnel inspect tools and holding, then inspect the first item before restarting production.

terms.meaning: A type used on top of a workbench.
Air raised to pressure for power or other uses.
Maintaining an item at a specified position or condition.
Checking the first item after starting or changing conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-035.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 10 comparing machines and 6 on cell entry. Make a machine/holding/hazard/first-piece table in 7 minutes, then explain automation and inspection in 3.
safety: Do not enter a robot enclosure from a stop indication alone or disable interlocks.
Control restarting and stored energy through prescribed tool-change and maintenance procedures.
mfg1-surface-lesson-035.summary:
Holding and hazards differ between machines.
Robots still require tool and first-piece checks.
Do not confuse stopping with authorization for safe entry.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.title: Separate pH records from oxidation and reduction
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.objective: Distinguish acidity and alkalinity from electron transfer; never judge chemical safety from a number alone.

paragraphs.title: Organize two different viewpoints
paragraphs.text: pH indicates the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution. In introductory examples involving dilute solutions near room temperature, neutrality is compared with approximately pH 7. Do not omit temperature and solution conditions and claim that every solution must lie between 0 and 14. Link the reading to solution identification, temperature and measurement method.

paragraphs.title: Explain electron transfer separately
paragraphs.text: Oxidation and reduction can also be explained through electron transfer: losing electrons is oxidation; gaining them is reduction. Rusting iron and combustion illustrate oxidation, but some reactions have no visible change. A low pH observation does not mean the same thing as a statement that a substance lost electrons.

paragraphs.title: Finding an unidentified solution
paragraphs.text: A workbench container bears only a pH number, without an ingredient name or measurement date. Even a near-neutral number does not identify harmless water. Keep the container identified, do not use it, and check the original record with the responsible person. Practice organizing sample records; do not experiment by mixing acids and alkalis.

terms.meaning: The property of an aqueous solution treated as having a lower pH than the neutral condition.
The property of an aqueous solution treated as having a higher pH than the neutral condition.
A change explained, among other ways, as losing electrons.
A change explained, among other ways, as gaining electrons.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Create records for three imaginary solutions and identify missing ingredient, temperature or measurement-date fields. Explain oxidation and reduction separately with electron arrows.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not mix chemicals or identify their contents by smell or bare-hand contact.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.summary: pH comparison and oxidation/reduction are different viewpoints. Record solution identity and conditions with the number; do not use an unknown solution on your own judgment.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.title: Distinguish the 3Rs by process stage
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.objective: Separate prevention, repeated use and material recovery while preserving quality and identification in resource circulation.

paragraphs.title: Think before disposal
paragraphs.text: Reduce prevents waste generation, reuse uses an item repeatedly, and recycle uses waste as a resource. These are not different names for the same task. Reducing unnecessary packaging and collecting used packaging to turn it back into material act at different stages.

paragraphs.title: Classify factory examples
paragraphs.text: Ordering only the required number of dividers prevents surplus. Inspecting and cleaning approved returnable trays for use again is reuse. Collecting non-reusable metal offcuts by material type for recovery is recycling. Reuse still requires conditions preventing contamination, damage and mixed part numbers.

paragraphs.title: Connect circulation with design and records
paragraphs.text: A circular economy links design, repair, reuse and resource recovery instead of only a one-way use-and-discard flow. A larger collection amount alone does not prove less waste was generated. Record generation and collection separately, and propose improvements without omitting protective packaging or safe segregation.

terms.meaning: Reducing unnecessary items or the amount of waste generated.
Using an item again after checking the conditions.
Using waste as a material or another resource.
An approach that circulates resources and reduces one-way mass disposal.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Classify returnable containers, metal offcuts and excess packaging under the 3Rs. Create separate generation/collection records and a checklist before reuse.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not mix waste contaminated with chemicals or oil without authorization; follow approved segregation and container-reuse methods.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.summary: The 3Rs act at different stages. Resource improvements must preserve product protection and identification of material type and contamination.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.title: Check a standard’s scope and edition against inspection requirements
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.objective: Distinguish product standards from management-system standards; do not accept individual products solely from names or marks.

paragraphs.title: Read what the standard addresses
paragraphs.text: Standards provide agreed requirements for quality, dimensions, performance and test methods. ISO is an organization concerned with international standardization; JIS means Japanese Industrial Standards. Standards covering products or labels address different subjects from standards covering an organization’s management system.

paragraphs.title: Separate management systems from individual acceptance
paragraphs.text: ISO 9001 concerns quality management, and ISO 14001 concerns environmental management. Information about an organization’s system does not replace required inspection of a particular part’s dimensions, damage or material. Instrument labels or marks likewise do not replace checks of condition, inspection status and measurement conditions.

paragraphs.title: Finding different editions
paragraphs.text: The edition referenced by an inspection sheet differs from the document on the workbench. Do not choose the newer-looking document yourself or judge from old memory alone. Confirm the edition specified for the product with the responsible person. Record document number, edition, scope and decision; do not change unconfirmed requirements yourself.

terms.meaning: Agreed requirements concerning quality, performance, dimensions or methods.
The range of items or activities to which a document or requirement applies.
An identifier distinguishing revisions or versions of a document.
Content that a product or activity is required to satisfy.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Compare the numbers, editions and subjects of two fictional documents and write a discrepancy report. Separate product-dimension checks from checks of an organizational management system in a table.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not alter documents or inspection conditions without authorization, or omit required checks solely because of an instrument label.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.summary: Check the subject and edition of a standard. Distinguish management-system or marking information from acceptance of individual products.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.title: Separate impact, bend and fatigue evaluation
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.objective: Distinguish sudden loading, condition after bending and repeated loading; do not substitute different test results.

paragraphs.title: Loads are applied differently
paragraphs.text: Impact tests examine energy absorbed when a specimen breaks under a sudden load. A pendulum apparatus uses the difference in its swing heights before and after fracture. Comparisons require matching specified specimen, temperature, notch and test-method conditions.

paragraphs.title: Examine bending and repetition separately
paragraphs.text: Bend tests inspect the outside and other specified parts of a specimen for cracks after bending under set conditions. Fatigue tests evaluate factors such as cycles to failure under repeated loading. Passing one slowly applied load does not prove survival under long-term repetition.

paragraphs.title: Read the test request carefully
paragraphs.text: A prototype support bracket raises concerns both about cracking after forming and repeated loads in service. Do not mark both as checked from a post-bend observation alone; organize suitable tests with the responsible person for each requirement. A textbook angle given for one material must not become an acceptance condition for every material.

terms.reading: きゅうしゅうエネルギー
terms.meaning: Energy taken up by a specimen during fracture or a similar event.
A test examining a specimen after bending under specified conditions.
Material failure caused by repeated loading.
The number of repeated applications of a similar load or event.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Match sudden collision, bending and repeated-motion requirements to test purposes. List three conditions to check before comparing results from different test conditions.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Pendulums, flying specimen fragments and trapping hazards exist. Actual tests must follow equipment procedures under trained personnel.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.summary: Impact, bend and fatigue tests differ in load and evaluation purpose. Always use results together with their specified conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.title: Relate a dial indicator’s difference to its reference dimension
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.objective: Read the indicator as a difference from a reference; check sign and mounting direction before calculating a dimension.

paragraphs.title: Read the indication as a reference difference
paragraphs.text: A dial indicator amplifies contact-point movement. In comparative measurement, set it against a reference such as a gauge block, replace that reference with the part, and read the difference. Do not mistake the small displayed difference for the part’s entire dimension.

paragraphs.title: Check direction and full revolutions
paragraphs.text: Align plunger movement with the change being measured and check for loose mounting or sticking. If the instrument has a short hand, include complete revolutions instead of reading the long hand alone. Confirm pushing direction, pointer rotation and positive/negative meaning from the instrument and setup instructions, not familiar appearance alone.

paragraphs.title: Add the difference to the reference
paragraphs.text: In a paper exercise, the reference is 30.00 mm and the specified signed difference is −0.04 mm. The part measures 30.00 − 0.04 = 29.96 mm. Record reference, sign, unit and measurement location together. If the reference setting shifts, do not conveniently edit numbers; follow the procedure to check the cause and affected parts.

terms.meaning: Measuring dimensions or other quantities using a difference from a reference.
The part that contacts the measured item and receives its movement.
The linearly moving part that holds the contact point.
A mark distinguishing positive and negative differences or values.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Calculate dimensions from a 25.00 mm reference with differences of +0.03 mm and −0.02 mm. Create mounting, reference, sign and unit fields and explain why reading only the long hand is insufficient.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not touch a moving workpiece with the contact point. Follow approved equipment/instrument procedures for mounting and reference setting.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.summary: Comparative measurement combines reference and difference. Check direction, sign, full revolutions and units before recording.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.title: Select comparative instruments for the measurement geometry
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.objective: Explain lever, cylinder and caliper forms and selection of their references.

paragraphs.title: Reaching the location is not enough
paragraphs.text: A lever-type indicator has a contact point that pivots like a lever. A cylinder gauge has a shape for comparative bore measurement. A dial caliper gauge has inside/outside-caliper-like contacts for hard-to-reach locations such as grooves. Check correct contact with the target surface as well as suitable range and resolution.

paragraphs.title: Combine reference and measuring direction
paragraphs.text: Comparative measurement requires setting against a specified reference. Learn the roles of gauge blocks and master rings, but do not treat a similarly named limit ring as a bore-setting reference automatically. For lever instruments, a mismatch between contact movement and the intended change causes error; verify the specified orientation.

paragraphs.title: Asking about a deep groove
paragraphs.text: Ordinary measuring faces cannot touch the intended position of a groove deep inside a hole. Do not record the visible entrance diameter as the groove diameter. Ask the responsible person about suitable contact geometry and reference. Record instrument, reference and position, and leave unmeasurable locations explicitly unverified.

terms.meaning: A form whose contact point or similar part pivots around a fulcrum.
An instrument shaped for comparative internal-diameter measurement.

terms.ja: ダイヤルキャリパーゲージ
terms.reading: ダイヤルキャリパーゲージ
terms.meaning: A dial instrument with caliper-shaped contact points.

terms.reading: きじゅんリングゲージ
terms.meaning: A ring-shaped reference used in comparative internal-diameter measurement.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Tabulate candidate instrument, contact surface and reference for a flat-surface change, bore and deep groove. Write two sentences requesting confirmation when measurement is impossible.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not force a probe into an inaccessible location or change instruments/references without authorization.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.summary: Match geometry, direction, range and reference. A reading from another contacted surface does not verify the target location.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.title: Separate master gauges from GO/NO-GO decisions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.objective: Distinguish reference comparison from limit checking and record gauge identification and both sides.

paragraphs.title: Check the reference’s role
paragraphs.text: Gauge blocks provide length references and master rings provide references such as bore size. Limit gauges check whether holes or shafts meet specified limits, generally using GO and NO-GO sides together. Even ring-shaped gauges have different roles as setting masters and acceptance gauges.

paragraphs.title: Do not judge from one side
paragraphs.text: In a basic smooth-hole example using the specified plug limit gauge, check that the GO side passes and the NO-GO side does not. If GO fails to enter, do not immediately blame machining alone: follow procedures to check part/gauge identification, contamination, damage and temperature. Never change the decision by forcing the gauge.

paragraphs.title: Threads and storage have their own instructions
paragraphs.text: Thread plug gauges serve internal threads; thread rings serve external threads. Apply the specified entry or turn-count criteria for thread NO-GO gauges rather than transferring a smooth-hole rule unchanged. Protect measuring faces and record reference dimension, gauge number, inspection state and result. Do not improvise burr removal or repair.

terms.meaning: A gauge checking whether a dimension is within specified limits.
The side that must pass under the specified conditions.
The side checked for non-passage or other specified behavior.
A plug-shaped thread gauge used to inspect internal threads.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.activity:
4 minutes: Check terms and the learning objective.
10 minutes: Read the text and distinguish similar concepts.
7 minutes: Write your decision and what remains unverified.
7 minutes: Create separate records for master and limit gauges. Enter both smooth-hole results and the extra thread-acceptance conditions to confirm; explain storage after use.
2 minutes: Summarize key points and workplace questions.
safety: Do not force insertion or screw-in. Follow material and instrument instructions for cleaning and corrosion protection.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.summary: Reference comparison and limit acceptance have different roles. Check identity, conditions and both GO/NO-GO results, including thread-specific criteria.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.title: Check drawing paper and lettering, then choose a drawing suited to the task
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.objective: Explain how paper and lettering affect readability, and the roles of detail, assembly and layout drawings.

paragraphs.title: Paper size and orientation
paragraphs.text: For the mechanical drawings covered in this textbook, A-series paper is preferred, in a size that clearly shows the object. Normally the long edge is horizontal; A4 may also be used in portrait orientation. A larger sheet does not make the information more accurate. On copied or reduced drawings, check that the lines and lettering remain clearly readable.

paragraphs.title: Read the character height
paragraphs.text: The size of lettering on a drawing is specified by its character height. The textbook lists 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm for kanji, and 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm for kana, letters and numbers. If a decimal point or part of a digit is illegible, do not guess and start work; request a legible approved drawing. Do not confuse enlargement or reduction during printing with a change to the stated dimension values.

paragraphs.title: Match the purpose of the work to the drawing
paragraphs.text: A detail drawing is for machining individual parts, an assembly drawing is for putting parts together, and a layout drawing shows matters such as equipment installation positions. Looking only at the hole dimensions of a part will not tell you where to install the equipment. Confirm the type of drawing and the object needed for the task, and ask the person responsible about missing information.

terms.meaning: Paper of a specified size used for drawing.
The height used to specify the size of drawing lettering.
A drawing that gives information needed to machine a part.
A drawing showing matters such as equipment installation positions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.activity:
4 min: Review the terms and learning objective.
10 min: Read the text and organize the relationship between drawing instructions and work.
7 min: Write your judgment for a concrete situation and the points still unconfirmed.
7 min: Make a table of the drawing types to give to a machining worker, an assembly worker and an installation worker. Sketch an A3 landscape and an A4 portrait page layout, and write an inquiry for an illegible decimal point.
2 min: Summarize the key points and what you want to confirm at work.
safety: Do not machine by guessing an illegible printed dimension. Put the relevant work on hold until a legible drawing has been checked.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.summary: Paper and lettering must be readable. Use drawings suited to machining, assembly or installation.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.title: Match viewing directions to view positions in third-angle projection
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.objective: Explain the positions of the top and side views in third-angle projection, and compare the front view with the other views.

paragraphs.title: Look at a solid object from several directions
paragraphs.text: A projection view represents the shape of a solid object on a plane. In third-angle projection, the top view, seen from above, is placed above the front view, and the right-side view, seen from the right, is placed to its right. First check the front view and the stated projection method so you do not confuse left and right on the paper with the direction from which the object is viewed.

paragraphs.title: The front view is chosen for shape and purpose
paragraphs.text: The front view is also called the principal view and clearly communicates shape and function. It is chosen with considerations such as the orientation in use for an assembly drawing, or the orientation during the main machining operation for a detail drawing. Avoiding too many hidden lines also matters. Do not assume without checking that the largest view is the front view.

paragraphs.title: Compare the same feature in three views
paragraphs.text: Imagine on paper a part with a hole on its top and a step on its side. The top view alone cannot establish the hole depth, so relate it to the front view or the sectional-view instructions. A projection-method symbol near the title block is another clue. If the arrangement does not match, do not mirror a view yourself; ask about the projection method and viewing direction.

terms.meaning: A plane representation of a solid object viewed from a particular direction.
A drawing method that places projection views in positions corresponding to their viewing directions.
The front view that mainly communicates shape and function.
A projection view of the object seen from above.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.activity:
4 min: Review the terms and learning objective.
10 min: Read the text and organize the relationship between drawing instructions and work.
7 min: Write your judgment for a concrete situation and the points still unconfirmed.
7 min: With the front view at the centre, mark the directions for viewing the top, right side and left side using arrows. Mark where the top and right-side views belong in third-angle projection, and write which additional views or instructions are needed to determine a hole depth.
2 min: Summarize the key points and what you want to confirm at work.
safety: Do not mirror a drawing in your own way for machining when its projection method or viewing direction is unclear. Confirm the correct orientation with the person responsible.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.summary: In third-angle projection, the view from above goes above, and the view from the right goes on the right. Check the method and front view before comparing views.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.title: Distinguish cut material from internal space in a sectional view
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.objective: Explain imaginary cutting and hatching, and relate hidden shapes to the other views.

paragraphs.title: It does not mean the object was actually cut
paragraphs.text: A sectional view represents the inside of an object by imagining a cut and removing the portion in front. It can make internal holes and steps easier to understand than using many hidden lines. It is a way of communicating shape, not a machining instruction to cut the actual product.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish hatching from a hole
paragraphs.text: The cut surface of material is generally hatched. For a cylindrical part, distinguish the material exposed by the cut from the space inside the bore. Do not mistake every hatched area for a hole, or treat the diagonal lines themselves as instructions to machine grooves. Check the dimensions and the other projection views together.

paragraphs.title: Not everything is drawn as cut in the same way
paragraphs.text: Some portions may be left unsectioned if cutting them would add no useful explanation and would instead make the drawing harder to understand. You therefore cannot conclude that every unhatched area is hollow. If the cutting position or the part concerned is unclear, check the assembly drawing, detail drawing and indicated extent of the section before explaining the internal shape.

terms.meaning: A view showing the inside of an object by imagining a cut.
The portion where material appears on an imaginary cutting plane.
Diagonal lines used to represent a cut surface in a section and similar features.
An internal space where material is absent.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.activity:
4 min: Review the terms and learning objective.
10 min: Read the text and organize the relationship between drawing instructions and work.
7 min: Write your judgment for a concrete situation and the points still unconfirmed.
7 min: Draw a hollow tube on paper and colour the cut material and the bore space differently. Explain why “no hatching always means a hole” is incorrect, and list three points to check in other views.
2 min: Summarize the key points and what you want to confirm at work.
safety: Do not start a cutting operation merely because a sectional view is shown. Distinguish machining instructions from graphical methods used to explain shape.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.summary: A sectional view uses an imaginary cut to communicate internal shape. Compare cut material, space and unsectioned portions with other views.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.title: Read the required length from dimension lines and values
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.objective: Explain the roles of dimension and extension lines, the units for length and angle, and how to inquire about duplicate indications.

paragraphs.title: Read the finished-part requirement
paragraphs.text: Dimensions give the information needed for a part’s function and manufacture and normally specify its finished dimensions. Repeating the same dimension unnecessarily can cause conflicting values after a change. Even if the drawing is printed large, read its stated dimensions rather than measuring the paper with a ruler as a substitute for the requirement.

paragraphs.title: The roles of two kinds of line
paragraphs.text: A dimension line corresponds to the indicated length or angle and has arrowheads or other end marks. Extension lines help show which positions the dimension runs between. Edge length, chord length, arc length and angle are not the same thing. Do not extract only the number; follow the end marks and extension lines to establish the feature concerned.

paragraphs.title: Check units and duplicate dimensions
paragraphs.text: Ordinary mechanical drawings may use millimetres for length without adding “mm” to every dimension value.
